title: Harnessing gasotransmitters for orthopaedic infection therapy: Mechanisms and advanced delivery platforms
abstract: Orthopaedic infections are increasingly prevalent in the aging population, posing a significant clinical and economic burden. Despite progress in antimicrobial therapies, challenges such as antibiotic resistance and superbug emergence persist. Gas therapy has emerged as a promising strategy for managing orthopaedic infections. Classical gasotransmitters-including nitric oxide (NO), carbon monoxide (CO), and hydrogen sulfide (HS)-exhibit antibacterial and immunomodulatory effects at controlled concentrations, though improper dosing may induce adverse effects. This review critically examines the dual mechanisms through which gasotransmitters combat infection while promoting orthopaedic regeneration. We also survey advanced delivery platforms-such as smart scaffolds, nano-reservoirs, and on-demand release systems-engineered for targeted gasotransmitter delivery to infected bone tissue. Finally, we discuss current limitations and future prospects, aiming to inspire novel biomaterial designs for targeted therapeutic delivery and to advance gas therapy as a viable option for orthopaedic infection treatment.

title: Bioprinted core-shell living material platform for spatially controlled encapsulation of Bacillus subtilis and sustained metabolite exchange
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) represents an escalating global health crisis, demanding alternative strategies to reduce resistant pathogen burden across environments. Microbe-based biocontrol is promising, yet effectively deploying it in practical settings remains challenging. In this study, we present a 3D bioprinted core-shell construct featuring a polyethylene glycol diacrylate (PEGDA) shell with tunable nanoscale porosity, encapsulating germinable spores of the biocontrol agentTH035. This configuration supports long-term spore viability while providing protection from common environmental stressors including UV-C irradiation, ethanol exposure, and desiccation over 4 weeks. The nanoporous PEGDA shell enables effective bacterial confinement while facilitating sufficient metabolite exchange forgermination and growth, as well as suppression of methicillin-resistant(MRSA) growth by approximately one order of magnitude. This approach demonstrates the feasibility of embeddingspores within engineered scaffolds for extended competitive functionality. The versatility and scalability of digital light processing (DLP) based bioprinting offers significant potential for tailored designs and high-throughput manufacturing. This proof-of-concept platform may find future applications in areas such as biomedical packaging, environmental sanitation, and built environment surface coatings, particularly in settings where intermittent moisture or nutrient availability can support spore germination and biocontrol activity.

title: Artificial intelligence catalyzes antimicrobial peptide design
abstract: With broad-spectrum, low resistance, and multifunctional properties, antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are promising therapeutic agents against drug-resistant pathogens, yet their discovery and optimization still remain challenging due to the complexity of sequence-function associations. Artificial intelligence (AI), through the construction of comprehensive data-driven models that assisted with miscellaneous learning strategies, enables de novo peptide design by learning latent representations inherent in peptide sequences as well as their biological properties to ensure physically plausible and biologically relevant predictions. Consequently, this paradigm enhances the likelihood of designing peptide candidates with significantly improved therapeutic potential, reducing resource-intensive trial-and-error processes and revealing the transformative impact of computational innovation in advancing next-generation therapeutics. Here, we provide a snapshot of this field and survey two modes of AI-driven technologies for AMP design, one concentrated on identifying whether current data possess antimicrobial activity (identification-oriented) and the other on generating AMP candidates with potential therapeutic properties (generation-oriented). We also highlight the challenges and limitations that still hinder AMP development even accelerated by AI, as well as the foreseeable prospects, from finer-grained explorations to model-driven data enrichment and model enhancement.

title: Antifungal mechanisms of volatile organic compounds and lactic acid produced by Lactiplantibacillus pentosus and their biocontrol application in fresh corn against Fusarium graminearum
abstract: Fusarium graminearum causes cereal spoilage and mycotoxin production. Currently, biocontrol microorganisms have emerged as a safe and promising strategy to manage the contamination of toxin-producing fungi in cereal grains. The primary objective was to elucidate the antifungal mechanism of an isolated strain of Lactiplantibacillus pentosus Q11 against F. graminearum and to evaluate the preservative effects of its cell-free supernatant (CFS) in fresh sweet corn. In vitro antifungal assays of L. pentosus Q11 showed strong antagonistic activity against F. graminearum, Aspergillus flavus, and Penicillium expansum, as well as the ability to reduce zearalenone. Moreover, whole-genome analysis revealed no genes related to virulence and antimicrobial resistance, and no hemolytic activity was observed, which suggested the potential safety of strain Q11. Moreover, the CFS of L. pentosus Q11 effectively inhibited the mycelial growth of F. graminearum, disrupted hyphal integrity, and induced fungal cell death. Moreover, 3 organic acids and 38 volatile compounds in the CFS of Q11 strain were identified by SPME-GC-MS and HPLC, in which 2-nonanone, 2-methylpyrazine, lactic acid, acetic acid were predominant compounds. The CFS and lactic acid combined with 2-nonanone severely damaged hyphae of F. graminearum, by disrupting cell membrane and wall, leading to leakage of intracellular substances, showing a synergistic antifungal effect of the two vital compounds. Subsequently, the treatments of CFS and combined agents significantly decreased 88.05% - 89.52% of fungal populations, and AFBand DON mycotoxin accumulation in fresh sweet corn after 12 days of storage compared to the control. The malondialdehyde content in the treated corn was decreased by 29.25% - 31.50%, consistent with the higher activities of POD and APX, thereby preserving their sensory attributes and nutritional quality. Metabolomic analysis revealed that L-glutamate, γ-glutamylcysteine, and oxidized glutathione were significantly downregulated in the glutathione metabolism pathway in the treated corn, indicating that CFS containing lactic acid and 2-nonanone could repress fungal growth and alleviate oxidative stress in fresh sweet corn. Overall, these findings demonstrate that L. pentosus Q11 with synergistic volatile organic compounds and lactic acid is a promising biocontrol agent in preserving fresh sweet corn.

abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is escalating in East Africa through close human-animal-environment interactions. Extended-spectrum beta-lactamases (ESBL) and carbapenemase-producingare clinically critical pathogens, yet local evidence is limited. This scoping review synthesizes evidence on ESBL and carbapenemase-producingin East Africa to inform One Health AMR control strategies. Following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, PubMed and Scopus were searched, identifying 279 records published between 2015 and 2025. After removing duplicates and screening, 185 articles were assessed for eligibility; 154 studies spanning human, animal and environmental sources met the inclusion criteria. Two reviewers independently extracted epidemiological, microbiological and molecular data in Covidence, including resistance genes and transmission evidence. The 154 included studies spanned 11 East African countries, led by Ethiopia ( = 55), Tanzania ( = 39) and Uganda ( = 22). Most studies (85.7%) were cross-sectional and human-focused (68.2%), with only 19 (12.3%) using a multi-sector One Health design. Overall, 21,554isolates were recovered from 74,700 samples. ESBL prevalence was reported in 117 studies (76.0%, median 46.8%) and carbapenemase prevalence in 65 (42.2%, median 3.3%), representing heterogeneous study-level estimates.predominated (89.9%), led by(26.1%); reported carbapenemase genes included,,andWhole-genome sequencing in 30 studies (19.5%) identified high-risk clones ST131, ST10, ST38 and ST410, though animal, food-chain and environmental sectors remained underrepresented. title: Dietary licorice improves carcass yield, hepatocellular protection, gut health, oxidative status, and cecal bacterial balance in broiler chickens
abstract: Over the past decade, phytotherapy such as licorice has attracted research as an alternative to antibiotic growth promoters in broiler production, driven by rising concerns over antimicrobial resistance. However, the consistency of its effects across productive, physiological, and health outcomes remains inconsistent. This meta-analysis quantitatively synthesized published experimental evidence on the effects of dietary licorice on growth performance, carcass yield, blood indices, visceral organs, oxidative status, intestinal morphology, and cecal bacterial balance in broiler chickens. A systematic literature search identified studies published between 2010 and 2025, and effect sizes were computed (Hedges'; 95% confidence interval). Pooled estimates were derived under the random-effects model using the restricted maximum likelihood estimator, with between-study heterogeneity characterized bythe-statistic. Univariable mixed-effects meta-regression was conducted to identify study-level moderators of treatment response, and publication bias was assessed using a funnel plot and the Rosenberg fail-safe N criterion. Dietary licorice did not affect feed intake or the feed conversion ratio, but it did increase body weight gain (BWG; SMD = 0.289; = 0.002), breast, thigh, gizzard, and bursa weights ( < 0.05). Gut integrity also improved with the villus height/crypt depth ratio (SMD = 0.931; = 0.041), andspp. counts (SMD = 0.266; = 0.003) increased, whilepopulations were suppressed (SMD = -1.737; < 0.001). Overall, the findings support that licorice enhances body weight gain, with route, duration, sex, and strain moderating efficacy.

abstract: ()is a globally pervasive and economically significant pathogen in bovine intramammary infections (IMIs) and is responsible for both clinical and subclinical mastitis. This study systematically investigated the global epidemiology offrom bovine IMIs, addressing antimicrobial resistance (AMR) amongthrough a meta-analysis. A total of 143 studies published between 2000 and 2025 were identified through comprehensive searches, which were based on predefined inclusion criteria. The data were systematically extracted, and the statistical analyses were performed in R (v4.5.2). The meta-analysis included 143 studies (145,457 samples), with a pooledprevalence of 24.78% and high heterogeneity (I = 99.51%). Subgroup analyses demonstrated significant heterogeneity in prevalence by study design, publication year, and region, with greater heterogeneity in cross-sectional studies (I>95%, < 0.001). Meta-regression identified sample size as a significant source of heterogeneity (β = -0.00002, = 0.02; R = 3.41%). The highest prevalence was reported in Cameroon (67%), Sri Lanka (64.3%), Indonesia (57%), and India (44%), with the lowest prevalence reported in Poland (0.7%), Taiwan (2.0%), Australia (5.5%), and New Zealand (5.3%). AMR was highest for doxycycline (70.7%), penicillin (65.2%), and ampicillin (62.8%); moderate to oxacillin (44.6%) and vancomycin (40.2%); and lowest for gentamicin (27.5%) and amikacin (18.3%). is highly prevalent in bovine IMIs worldwide, with marked regional heterogeneity and substantial resistance to commonly used antimicrobials, emphasizing the urgent need for targeted surveillance, prudent antimicrobial use, and improved mastitis control strategies at the global and regional levels.

N-acetylcysteine as an adjunct to antibiotics against bacterial biofilms: A systematic review of in vitro evidence
abstract: N-acetylcysteine (NAC) is investigated as an antibiotic adjunct, but acidity, formulation and experimental context complicate interpretation. We evaluated comparative in-vitro evidence while distinguishing biofilm prevention, established-biofilm treatment and resistance evolution. MEDLINE/PubMed, Embase, Scopus and Web of Science were searched through August 2026, with supplementary searching. Extraction distinguished NAC preparation and exposure pH, medium, hydrodynamics, NAC-alone controls, treatment intent and interaction methodology. Results were synthesized by experimental context, regimen, phase and endpoint without pooling or whole-study efficacy voting. Fifty-five studies were included: 7 evaluated combination exposure during formation only, 37 after establishment only, 9 both, and 2 resistance evolution. NAC-alone arms were documented in 39 studies, partial or formulation-specific in 9, and not identified in 7. Only two studies included a continuous-flow model. Selected combinations improved biofilm-associated outcomes, but intrinsic-acidic and neutralized preparations, biomass and viability endpoints, and planktonic versus biofilm interaction tests were not interchangeable. Liposomal and catheter-lock findings differed by dose matching, isolate and control set. Polymyxin findings varied with organism, resistance background, medium and exposure; rifampicin-alone and rifampicin-containing multidrug comparators addressed different questions. NAC is a context-dependent experimental adjunct, not an established class-wide antibiotic potentiator. The evidence does not support clinical antibiotic dose reduction or routine NAC combination therapy. Translation requires controlled final exposure pH, matched monotherapy and formulation controls, clinically relevant background regimens, viable-burden and regrowth outcomes, and resistance monitoring.

Combating antimicrobial resistance through multimodal data via artificial intelligence
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) poses a critical global health challenge, leading to substantial mortality and economic losses without science-based interventions. Conventional approaches to combating AMR have important limitations in addressing this escalating threat. Recent advances in AI, including deep learning, large language models, and protein language models, provide new opportunities to integrate multimodal data for AMR research. However, evidence remains uneven, with many approaches limited to computational benchmarking rather than real-world validation. Here, we critically review AI applications in AMR, focusing on rapid diagnosis, therapeutic discovery, and clinical decision support. AI-based diagnostic models can identify resistant pathogens and predict resistance profiles, but most lack prospective clinical evaluation. AI-assisted drug discovery and alternative therapies have generated promising candidates, although most remain at computational, in vitro, or early preclinical stages. Large language models may support decision-making, but their clinical use remains preliminary. Successful translation of AI into clinical and One Health practice will require representative datasets, independent validation, prospective evaluation, and robust governance.

Strengthening One Health Antimicrobial Resistance Surveillance in Bangladesh: Insights from the Fleming fund country grant
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is an escalating global public health concern, with particularly severe implications for low and middle-income countries such as Bangladesh. In Bangladesh context, fragmented surveillance systems and the extensive use of antimicrobials across human, animal, and aquaculture sectors contribute to the rapid emergence and spread of resistance. Strengthening integrated surveillance through a One Health approach is therefore crucial to support effective policy development and response strategies. This review outlines the policy, implementation, and key outcomes of the Fleming Fund Country Grant in Bangladesh between 2020 and 2025. It draws upon multiple data sources, including programme reports, routine AMR surveillance data, laboratory capacity-building initiatives, and stakeholder engagement activities across human, animal, aquaculture, and environmental sectors. Through this initiative, a coordinated national AMR surveillance network was established, comprising 20 laboratories across multiple sectors, including three designated national reference laboratories. The initiative strengthened surveillance through the introduction of standardized protocols and SOPs, improved diagnostic capacity, skilled workforce, and implementation of laboratory quality assurance systems, including EQA and NEQA. These measures enhanced the accuracy, consistency, and reliability of AMR surveillance data. In addition, the establishment of a national AMR data integration platform facilitated real time data sharing and evidence-based decision-making. A total of 208,346 bacterial isolates were analyzed, with AST results reported to the AMR dashboard across the human, and animal, health sectors. Overall, the Fleming Fund programme has made a substantial contribution to strengthening integrated AMR surveillance in Bangladesh by operationalizing a One Health framework. Continued political commitment, increased domestic investment, and the institutionalization of surveillance systems will be essential to sustain these gains and ensure long-term resilience against AMR.

Microfluidic-assembled curcumin ionizable lipid nanoparticles enhance aqueous delivery and antibiofilm activity against Staphylococcus aureus
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance and biofilm-associated infections demand novel therapeutic strategies. Curcumin is a natural polyphenol with broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity; however, its clinical utility is fundamentally constrained by negligible aqueous solubility and limited biofilm penetration. Here, we used microfluidic assembly to prepare curcumin-loaded ionizable lipid nanoparticles (Cur@LNP) with three clinically established ionizable lipids (SM-102, MC-3, and ALC-0315). The resulting formulations were uniform, with hydrodynamic diameters of approximately 90 nm and polydispersity indices near 0.1. Relative to free curcumin in DMSO, Cur@LNP lowered the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) 8-fold and the minimum bactericidal concentration (MBC) 16-fold against planktonic, and markedly reduced viable biofilm-resident cells at matched concentrations. Scanning electron microscopy showed that Cur@LNP treatment remodeled mature biofilms into irregular, debris-rich aggregates with reduced extracellular matrix coverage. Notably, antimicrobial performance was indistinguishable across the three structurally distinct ionizable lipids at every concentration tested. Within this in vitro, single-strain system, the antibiofilm effect is therefore dominated by the cargo (curcumin) rather than by ionizable-lipid chemistry, and it is most likely attributed to enhanced aqueous solubilization of curcumin rather than to engagement of the lipid headgroup with the biofilm matrix. These results position microfluidic-assembled ionizable LNPs as a reproducible, scalable solubilization platform for poorly water-soluble natural antimicrobials.

abstract: Commensal small mammals, such as rats and shrews, are recognized reservoirs for numerous zoonotic pathogens; however, their role in pathogen circulation at transport hubs remains underexplored. This study employs shotgun metagenomic sequencing to characterize microbial communities and assess zoonotic potential in tissue samples from commensal small mammals captured at Bangkok Port, an international cargo shipping hub in Thailand between June and August 2025. Following host read depletion, taxonomic profiling was performed to identify bacterial taxa of public health relevance, including sequences assigned tospp.,,, and. The virulence factor and antibiotic resistance gene profiles revealed that some of these pathogens have pathogenic potential and are related to drug-resistant bacteria. In addition,was identified as a shared taxon among rats, shrews, and their associated fleas. The findings support the ecological roles of mammalian hosts and their ectoparasites as reservoirs for pathogens of public health concern. These results emphasize the need to strengthen surveillance programs for commensal small mammals to monitor and mitigate the spread of transboundary pathogens at international maritime gateways.

Wild boar as a sentinel species for ecosystem health surveillance: A review
abstract: Sentinel surveillance uses selected species that are widely distributed, easily sampled, and exposed to multiple health threats as indicators of ecosystem health. The Eurasian wild boar () is a broadly distributed game species that meets these conditions. We conducted a systematic review to assess the suitability of the wild boar as a sentinel or indicator species for monitoring health hazards relevant to ecosystem health, focusing on the hazards monitored, methods, justification for use, perceived performance, limitations, and proposed improvements. We identified 86 studies explicitly framing the wild boar as a sentinel species, covering a wide range of hazards, including 30 pathogens, 44 environmental contaminants, two biological toxins and 13 antimicrobial resistance (AMR) indicators. It was used to monitor pathogens (57%), environmental contaminants (31.4%), AMR (12.8%), and biological toxins (3.5%). Research effort was concentrated in Europe (84.9%) and relied mostly on hunted animals (90.7%). Wild boar were frequently selected as sentinels due to their previous use as indicators of ecosystem health in the literature, omnivorous diet, wide distribution, and accessibility as game species. However, hunting-based sampling may introduce biases, while post-mortem conditions and ecological variability may affect results. Despite this, 74.4% of studies supported their use as sentinels, particularly for pathogens and environmental contaminants. In contrast, their perceived suitability for AMR was more variable, and no quality assessment was available for biological toxins. Overall, wild boar sentinel surveillance is considered logistically efficient and valuable for monitoring ecosystem health hazards. However, its effectiveness is context-dependent and influenced by methodological and ecological limitations. Improving surveillance design through systematic sampling, alternative sample sources (e.g., found-dead animals or non-invasive methods), integration of multi-species data, and inclusion of covariates could enhance the reliability of findings within a One Health framework.

title: Global spread of carbapenem-resistant Providencia driven by high-risk lineages and plasmid co-evolution
abstract: Carbapenem-resistant(CRP) is a formidable opportunistic pathogen with extensive drug resistance, posing an increasing threat to human, animal, and environmental health. However, its global genomic epidemiology and resistome-plasmidome co-evolution within a One Health context remain poorly understood. Here, we conducted a comprehensive population genomic and plasmid analysis of 1197 CRP isolates from 35 countries spanning 2012-2025. We reclassified the CRP population into ninespecies, identifyingandas established epidemic species alongside the rapid emergence ofand. We pinpointed 2019 as a critical inflection point, marking the transition from endemic stability to rapid global epidemic expansion (80.8% isolates in 2019-2025). Ten intercontinentally disseminated high-risk sequence types (e.g., ST46, ST79), each with strict species-ST specificity, were responsible for global spread. Thegene (62.4% prevalence) was the predominant carbapenem gene, exhibiting strong geographic and species specificity and mutual exclusion with other major carbapenem genes. Plasmids encoded approximately 80% of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) genes, with 78.0% of these plasmids belonging to 75 stable clusters. These clusters evolved a dual specialist-generalist strategy, with the broad-host-range cluster 72 mediating interspecies AMR transmission and cluster 7 acting as a super-vector carrying six carbapenem genes. Importantly, CRP circulated across interconnected human, animal, and environmental reservoirs, with distinct host-associated species distributions suggesting ecological niche adaptation and potential cross-host dissemination of resistance determinants. These findings demonstrate that the global expansion of CRP is driven by the combined evolution of high-risk clones and mobile genetic elements across interconnected ecological sectors, underscoring the need for integrated One Health surveillance and coordinated interventions spanning clinical, veterinary, agricultural, and environmental settings.

abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) has intensified in recent years, raising concerns about the potential impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on AMR dynamics. However, the influence of pandemic on the enviromental occurrence and dissemination of antibiotic-resistant genes (ARGs) remains under investigation. Wastewater-based epidemiology (WBE) provides an integrated view of community-level AMR dynamics, yet long-term assessments spanning the pandemic period remain limited. This study investigated the occurrence, temporal patterns, and seasonal behavior of two clinically relevant carbapenemase genes,and, in raw wastewater from the Attica region over a five-year period (July 2021-September 2025). A sensitive and specific 3-plex qPCR assay was developed and analytically validated for the simultaneous quantification of,, and 16S rRNA, the latter serving as a stable bacterial load indicator. Across the monitoring period,was consistently detected, showing a steady increase and reaching its highest concentrations in 2023, whileexhibited intermittent but pronounced surges, particularly in 2023. Comparison with community SARS-CoV-2 viral loads suggest temporal association with AMR signatures in wastewater. Seasonal analysis showed non-uniform patterns, with atypical warm-season peaks of both ARGs in 2023-2024 and a return to classical autumn-winter peaks in 2025, suggesting a gradual restoration of pre-pandemic seasonality. To our knowledge, this is among the first long-term WBE studies to characterize post-COVID-19 shifts in ARG occurrence and seasonality. The results demonstrate that the pandemic period was associated with elevated and fluctuating ARG levels in the urban wastewater system, emphasizing the need for sustained AMR monitoring. These findings address critical knowledge gaps in environmental AMR surveillance and support the integration of WBE into public health strategies aimed at mitigating AMR dissemination.

title: Prevalence of antimicrobial-resistant Escherichia coli as an indicator bacterium in livestock and companion animals in Mongolia
Genomic epidemiology to investigate the origins and zoonotic implications of antibiotic-resistant Escherichia coli on beef and lamb meat sold by independent butchers in Wales
abstract: Many studies have identified antibiotic resistant (ABR)on meat. Appropriate hand hygiene and cooking practices should minimize the risk of gastrointestinal colonisation with ABRfound on meat, and the subsequent chance of causing resistant opportunistic extraintestinal infection. There are large gaps in our understanding of the prevalence, origins and zoonotic potential of ABRfound on meat, however, and particularly for meat reared in extensive farming systems. Wales is a devolved nation within the United Kingdom having large populations of extensively-reared sheep and beef cattle. To help address knowledge gaps around ABRon extensively reared meat, therefore, beef mince and lamb loin/leg steaks/chops were purchased from 50 (beef) and 46 (lamb) independent butchers across Wales. Following enrichment culture, 200 g meat samples were found to be positive forresistant to amoxicillin (31% positivity), streptomycin (28%), spectinomycin (29%), amoxicillin-clavulanate (11%), 3rd generation cephalosporins (2%) and fluoroquinolones (5%). Phylogenetic analysis confirmed that Welsh lamb meat ABRisolates ( = 78) are more closely related to those found in faecal samples collected around sheep ( = 352) than around beef cattle ( = 361) on Welsh farms. This suggests that faecal contamination at or around slaughter is their primary origin. We found no closely related meat/infection clones (<20 SNPs distant and the same antibiotic resistance genes) when comparing ABRfrom Welsh meat ( = 91) and those causing extraintestinal infections in people ( = 2387) in an English region bordering Wales. We conclude, therefore, that the wider zoonotic implications of finding ABRon beef and lamb meat sold at independent butchers in Wales are small, though a more geographically and temporarily contemporaneous survey is warranted to address this further.

title: Genomic insights into activated antimicrobial resistance of in situ hospital-wastewater biofilm
Risk ranking and antimicrobial resistance of Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli of bovine origin
Remote realities: In-depth conversations on antimicrobial stewardship in remote Indigenous communities using a One Health approach
Sewage surveillance for assessing clinical antibiotic resistance prevalence: Combining metagenomic and phenotypic data
abstract: Surveillance of antibiotic resistance in clinical isolates is a cornerstone for the management of bacterial infections but is limited in large parts of the world, often due to lack of resources. Sewage surveillance has been proposed as a promising, resource-efficient complement to the traditional surveillance approach based on samples from many individual patients. Both phenotypic data on resistance in sewage isolates and abundance of antibiotic resistance genes in sewage have been shown to correlate with resistance prevalence in clinical isolates. Here, we aimed to directly compare and combine an isolate-based and a gene-based sewage surveillance approach to evaluate what best can reflect clinical resistance rates. The two approaches, based on susceptibility testing of collectedisolates and metagenomic sequencing, respectively, were applied to municipal sewage samples collected in ten European countries. The data generated was related to available data on resistance to aminopenicillins, fluoroquinolones, third generation cephalosporins and aminoglycosides prevalence in clinicalisolates using beta regression models. None of the tested individual predictors were superior across all four investigated classes of antibiotics. For modelling of aminopenicillin resistance, a clearly higher Rvalue was obtained when isolate-based and gene-based data was combined as predictors, also after adjusting for the number of included variables. We conclude that there could be a value of including both isolate- and gene-based sewage data for predictions of resistance rates in clinical isolates, while emphasizing the value of linking predictors to specific species and classes of antibiotics.

title: Clonal diversity, virulence factors and antibiotic resistance genes of Enterococcus faecalis and Klebsiella pneumoniae from urban rats in Malaysia
abstract: Peridomestic rats serve as important carriers of zoonotic pathogens, including multidrug-resistant bacteria such asand. However, information on the clonal diversity, antibiotic resistance, and virulence of these pathogens in wild urban rats remains limited, particularly in tropical settings. This study investigatedandin urban rats from wet markets across four Malaysian states. A total of 277 rats (, = 177;, = 100) were trapped, and lung tissues were processed for bacterial isolation. Isolates were identified by 16S rDNA sequencing and examined for antibiotic susceptibility, resistance genes, and virulence factors using PCR. Clonal relationships were determined through multilocus sequence typing (MLST). Nineteenand sevenisolates were recovered. Allisolates carried multiple virulence factors (,,, and), and four tetracycline-resistant isolates possessed,, and. Five novelsequence types (ST730 - ST734) were identified. Allisolates carried the SHV gene; two also harbored FOX, and two possessedandvirulence factors. Two novelSTs (ST2641 and ST2642) were detected. Phylogenetic analyses revealed that both species displayed diverse sequence types scattered across global lineages. These findings suggest that urban rats may act as potential carriers of virulent and antibiotic-resistantand. These findings support the inclusion of urban rats in future One Health surveillance programs investigating antimicrobial resistance and virulent bacterial pathogens.

title: Virulence attenuation in ST11-K64 Klebsiella pneumoniae explains its divergent clinical manifestation from ST23-K1
Design, synthesis, and antibacterial activity study of pyrroloquinazoline diamine derivatives
Antimicrobial resistance patterns and polymicrobial co-detection characteristics of vaginal Group B Streptococcus in pregnant women: a retrospective study
Genetic determinants of hypervirulence with attenuated pathogenicity in a bla(NDM-1)-encoding Klebsiella pneumoniae causing neonatal sepsis
Copper-coated carbon nanotube surfaces for inhibiting biofilm formation by Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa
abstract: Biofilm-associated infections caused by clinically important pathogens such as() and() remain a major challenge in healthcare settings due to enhanced antimicrobial resistance and persistence. In recent years, copper-coated carbon nanotubes (Cu-CNTs) have gained considerable attention as promising antimicrobial nanomaterials for preventing biofilm formation on medical devices and hospital-associated surfaces. This review summarizes recent advances in the development and application of Cu-CNT-based antimicrobial coatings, with an emphasis on their antibacterial and antibiofilm activities against Gram-positive and Gram-negative pathogens. The synergistic combination of the high surface-area-to-volume ratio of CNTs and the potent antimicrobial properties of copper (Cu) ions enhances microbial inhibition. Previous studies suggest that Cu-CNTs interfere with initial bacterial adhesion, inhibit biofilm maturation, and disrupt established biofilms through mechanisms involving oxidative stress generation, membrane destabilization, and cellular damage. Furthermore, the review discusses the physicochemical characteristics, antimicrobial mechanisms, biomedical applications, and potential challenges associated with Cu-CNT coatings, including toxicity and biocompatibility concerns. Overall, Cu-CNT-based coatings represent a promising strategy for developing durable antimicrobial surfaces to control chronic biofilm-associated infections and reduce healthcare-associated contamination.

title: Antibacterial and antibiofilm evaluation of biogenic ternary CuO-AgO-MgO nanocomposite against clinical isolates of carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae
Accelerating Shigella vaccines: from decades of research to global access
'Responsive Dialogues', an engagement framework for antimicrobial resistance: a cross-country qualitative evaluation in Thailand and Malawi

Invasive Pneumococcal Disease burden, clinical characteristics, serotypes' distribution, immunization status and antimicrobial resistance: Evidence from 12-year hospital-based surveillance and cost analysis
A synopsis of competence-regulated virulence in Streptococcus pneumoniae
Phylogenomic framework and virulence gene boundaries of emerging Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli O118 informed by the comprehensive profiling of 359 O118 genomes
Preventive strategies for recurrent urinary tract infections in premenopausal women: A scoping review
Genomic insights into multidrug-resistant bacteria: Emergence of mcr-1.1 in Escherichia coli, bla(KPC-2) in Klebsiella pneumoniae and Serratia marcescens from clinical settings
Metagenomic next-generation sequencing for pathology-suspected fungal infections at rare anatomical sites: a case series
Acinetobacter baumannii: Mechanisms of antibiotic resistance, quorum sensing regulation, and current therapeutic strategies
Lactobacillus acidophilus membrane vesicles demonstrate antimicrobial and antibiofilm activity against Streptococcus mutans - an in vitro and in vivo study
Synergistic antibacterial activity and mechanism of arginine combined with florfenicol against Escherichia coli
Differential modulation of gentamicin antibacterial activity by vitamin B12 and vitamin D3 against Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria: an in vitro-in silico study
Extending digital biology: Bacterial survival and morphological heterogeneity under antibiotic stress
abstract: Bacterial morphology is modified by antibiotic stress depending on the antibiotic mechanism of action, while changes in morphology can contribute to cell survival. Here we present a workflow that generates morphological signatures for the progeny of individual bacterial cells across 168 antibiotic conditions. The workflow uses stationary microfluidic droplets to encapsulate and grow bacteria and confocal microscopy to image the droplet content. A custom image analysis pipeline labels morphologies in a subset of images to train a neural network. The network yields multidimensional morphological signatures from 82,000 droplets, showing the co-existence of different morphologies even for the progeny of individual cells. The signatures differ with antibiotic type and concentration, providing a way to distinguish antibiotics by their mode of action. Combined with digital detection of bacterial survival within droplets, this workflow provides a quantitative platform to investigate antibiotic resistance and identify the antimicrobial activity of unknown compounds.

title: Artificial plastic substrate for tracking and exploring antimicrobial-resistant bacteria transmission pathways in aquatic ecosystems
abstract: Investigating the persistence and dissemination of antibiotic-resistant bacteria (ARBs) in aquatic ecosystems is challenging because conventional methods require large volumes of water, particularly difficult to collect in regions affected by climate-related stress. This study developed and evaluated artificial plastic substrates (APSs) as an effective sampling tool and assessed the potential role of plastic as a transmission vector for ARBs. Five monthly sampling campaigns were conducted at three sites along the Arrone River. A total of 127 ARBs, including extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL)-producing Enterobacteriaceae andspp., were isolated from APSs and raw water (RW) and characterized at the microbiological and molecular levels. APSs recovered more ARBs than RW and captured key antibiotic resistance genes, including class 1 integrons and genes associated with β-lactam, carbapenem, tetracycline, sulfonamide, aminoglycoside, chloramphenicol, and efflux pump-mediated resistance. Overall, APSs proved to be an efficient, cost-effective, reproducible, and minimally invasive tool for monitoring ARBs and ARGs in aquatic ecosystems.

title: High-risk ARGs in environmental E. coli from the Taihu Lake watershed
Antibiotic resistance genes in aquaculture: Molecular detection, environmental dynamics, and biological control strategies
Bridging soil resistome and clinical inference: A four-tier evidentiary framework
Harnessing hydrogel technology for advanced periodontitis therapy: A multifunctional approach to oral health restoration
abstract: Periodontitis is a bacterially driven inflammatory disease that can lead to tooth mobility and tooth loss. Conventional non-surgical therapy, antibiotics, and surgery may be limited by residual subgingival biofilms, antimicrobial resistance, and variable clinical outcomes. This review synthesizes recent studies of hydrogel-based systems for local periodontal therapy, focusing on stimuli-responsive release mechanisms, cargo-loading approaches, and regenerative outcomes in relevant animal models. Across these studies, hydrogels function as localized delivery matrices that can prolong retention at periodontal defects, regulate therapeutic exposure, and support tissue repair. We further evaluate translational considerations, including degradation behavior, long-termstability, and immunocompatibility. These findings position hydrogels as adaptable platforms for more precise periodontitis management and identify priorities for preclinical optimization before clinical translation.

title: Microbiota-constrained bacterial density limits phage infection in the gut and allows persistence of susceptible cells
abstract: With the rise of antibiotic resistance, bacteriophage-based treatments against bacterial infections have regained momentum. However, phage therapy has so far shown only moderate success in complex environments like the mammalian gut, where phages are particularly promising tools for microbiome engineering and specific elimination of opportunistic pathogens. Here, we use different murine models of intestinal colonization to quantitatively assess the minimal population size of susceptiblecells that is required for phage replication in the gut (replication threshold). We found that the composition of the intestinal microbiota is a key factor shaping phage-bacteria interactions by restricting the carrying capacity of susceptible host cells. We further demonstrate that the replication threshold enables coexistence of susceptible and resistant bacteria in phage-treated mice, with implications for phage-based applications in complex environments like the gut.

title: Fate and effects of emerging contaminants during anaerobic digestion of organic wastes: Effective exposure, mechanisms and intervention strategies
abstract: Methane recovery from anaerobic digestion can be held back by emerging contaminants, and so can the range of uses open to the digestate. This review covers pharmaceuticals, disinfectants, per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, micro- and nanoplastics, and selected engineered nanomaterials in sludge, manure, food waste, and industrial residues. The synthesis draws on comparisons within individual studies to examine how contaminant form, contact with biomass, and exposure duration shape responses at individual steps of anaerobic digestion. Reversals between stimulation and inhibition appear in dose series for perfluorobutanesulfonate and for bisphenol A. Inhibition can also emerge once exposure is prolonged, at a point that short-term tests do not reach. Among the interventions examined, gains in methane recovery do not necessarily coincide with gains in contaminant transformation or in antibiotic-resistance outcomes. Two separate tasks are involved: restoring inhibited digestion, and improving contaminant transformation without losing methane production. Products left behind by transformation can retain biological activity. Phase-resolved mass balances are a way to tell genuine destruction apart from transfer into concentrates and spent media. Engineering comparisons show that a benefit can fade even when the material is still in place, and that a higher electrical input can return less additional methane. Intervention selection should account for the limiting conversion step, the residues relevant to the intended use of digestate, and the energy, materials and maintenance needed to sustain treatment.

title: [Public Health as an Elective in the Final Clinical Year in Baden-Württemberg, Germany: Results of a Mixed-Methods Study on Elective Evaluation and Development of an Evaluation Instrument]
abstract: In light of global challenges such as pandemics, social inequality, antibiotic resistance, and climate change, public health perspectives are becoming increasingly important in medical care. However, medical education remains predominantly focused on individual patient care. Content related to public health and practical insights into public health services (PHS) have so far been incorporated into the curriculum only to a limited extent. Since November 2023, it has been possible to take a public health elective at six pilot teaching local public health authorities (LHA) in Baden-Württemberg, Germany. The purpose of this study is to evaluate the implementation of this public health elective. Using an exploratory sequential mixed-methods design, qualitative individual interviews were conducted with students and supervisors from six pilot LHA. Based on these findings, a questionnaire instrument for the long-term evaluation of the public health elective was developed and piloted. Five students and five staff members from LHA were interviewed. Eight of the 14 students participated in the survey. The public health elective was rated positively overall by both students and supervisors. The students surveyed highlighted the structured orientation, the dedicated supervision, and the flexibility in rotation planning and working hours. All students reported gaining a good overview of LHA activities. Six out of eight students gave the highest grade, and all will recommend it to others. Practical competencies were acquired primarily in the Child and Adolescent Health Service, the HIV/STI service, and in infection control. Criticisms included the logbook, which was perceived as too extensive and not very practice-oriented, as well as the cross-site organization of the public health elective support classes. The results suggest that the public health elective can help raise awareness of PHS and help medical students with their career planning. Given the global challenges, the public health elective can help incorporate public health perspectives into medical education and provide hands-on experience in this field. Furthermore, there are indications that the introduction of the public health elective may also stimulate organizational development within LHA. Due to the small sample size and potential selection bias, generalizability of findings is limited.

title: Genomic epidemiology and transmission dynamics of Acinetobacter baumannii: Comparison of clinical and wastewater isolates
abstract: This study characterized the epidemiological, phenotypic, and genomic dynamics of Acinetobacter baumannii across inpatient, outpatient, hospital environmental, and diverse wastewater habitats from January to December 2025. Bacterial detection exhibited pronounced seasonal variations and habitat heterogeneity, with wastewater showing the highest prevalence and summer marking the peak period. High-touch surfaces represented the core hospital contamination nodes, and healthcare workers faced potential risks of carbapenem-resistant A. baumannii (CRAB) colonization. Notably, CRAB and multidrug-resistant strains appeared confined to clinical niches, where the dominant ST2and ST164clones stably harbored abundant carbapenemases, disinfectant resistance genes, and virulence factors. Anthropogenic antibiotic and sanitizer selective pressures likely drive their high multiple antibiotic resistance index (MARI) phenotypes. Conversely, wastewater strains were predominantly pan-susceptible (MARI < 0.2) but enriched with novel sequence types (STs) and rare resistance genes, suggesting their role as a natural reservoir for genetic diversification. Core-genome SNP transmission networks indicated high-density intra-hospital cross-transmission and occult inter-hospital dissemination, while capturing potential bidirectional cross-habitat spillover events. Mechanistically, conjugative plasmids, insertion sequences (IS256/IS3/IS66), and active prophages mediated resistance and virulence recombination in clinical strains. Meanwhile, wastewater strains might utilize the ISNCY family to undergo environmental adaptation, with integrons playing a minor role in resistance spread. This study uncovers the divergent evolutionary pathways of A. baumannii, providing critical genomic evidence for integrated clinical-environmental management to mitigate the cross-niche dissemination of antimicrobial resistance.

title: Acquired antimicrobial resistance in clinical and hospital-environment isolates in onco-haematology: Detection of blaVIM-4/blaPER-1 in Stenotrophomonas maltophilia and aac(6')-Ib-cr/sul2/dfrA1 in Burkholderia cepacia
abstract: Stenotrophomonas maltophilia and Burkholderia cepacia are opportunistic saprophytic bacteria that have emerged as important pathogens in immunocompromised patients. The objective of this study was to characterize antimicrobial resistance determinants in clinical and environmental isolates of S. maltophilia and B. cepacia and to assess their potential clinical relevance. A total of 71 clinical isolates of S. maltophilia and B. cepacia, collected between 2018 and 2022, and 25 environmental isolates collected in 2023, were identified using the Analytical Profile Index 20NE (API 20NE). Antimicrobial susceptibility was assessed by the disc diffusion method and the Epsilometer test (E-test). The double-disc synergy test screened for extended-spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL) activity; resistance genes were detected by polymerase chain reaction (PCR), and the genetic context of blaVIM-4 was investigated by whole-genome sequencing (WGS). A total of 51 S. maltophilia and 12 B. cepacia strains were resistant to at least one antibiotic. An ESBL phenotype was detected in 34 S. maltophilia and six B. cepacia strains. We report the detection of blaVIM-4 and blaPER-1 in S. maltophilia, and of aac(6')-Ib-cr, sul2, and dfrA1 in B. cepacia. Genomic analysis suggested a probable chromosomal location of blaVIM-4 within a class 1 integron, alongside aac(6')-II, dfrA1, and sul1, flanked by TnpR- and TnpA-family transposases, in an ST78 S. maltophilia strain. Although the S. maltophilia species is intrinsically resistant to carbapenems, the detection of blaVIM-4 highlights the importance of further investigation to study the potential mobilization and horizontal transfer of this gene to susceptible species in clinical settings.

title: Evaluation of antibiotic resistance profiles, biofilm formation capacity and molecular detection of resistance genes in clinical P. aeruginosa isolates recovered from hospitalized patients in Ilam, Iran
abstract: P. aeruginosa is a leading cause of healthcare-associated infections and is recognized by the WHO as a critical priority pathogen due to its intrinsic and acquired resistance mechanisms and its remarkable capacity for biofilm formation. This study aimed to evaluate antibiotic resistance profiles, biofilm formation capacity, and the molecular detection of resistance genes in clinical P. aeruginosa isolates recovered from hospitalized patients in Ilam, Iran. A total of 44 non-duplicate P. aeruginosa isolates were collected from urine, blood, and sputum specimens between November 2023 and August 2024. Identification used standard microbiological and biochemical tests. Antimicrobial susceptibility was determined by Kirby-Bauer disk diffusion following CLSI guidelines, and colistin MIC was determined by broth microdilution. Biofilm formation was assessed using a microtiter plate assay with crystal violet staining. Major resistance genes, including β-lactamases (-GES,-CTX,-SHV,-TEM), metallo-β-lactamases (-NDM,-VIM,-IMP), and fluoroquinolone resistance determinants (parC, parE), were detected via PCR. The isolates exhibited high resistance rates to aztreonam (100%), gentamicin (68.2%), and imipenem (59.1%), while amikacin remained the most effective agent (95.5% susceptible). Following broth microdilution, colistin resistance was only 2.3%. Molecular analysis revealed that-GES (100%) and parC (95.5%) were the most prevalent resistance genes. followed by-CTX (55.5%),-SHV (45.5%),-TEM (45.5%), parE (36.4%),-NDM (13.6%),-VIM (13.6%), and-IMP (4.5%). Biofilm formation was observed in all isolates: 68.2% weak, 31.8% moderate; no strong producers were identified. A significant association was found between anatomical specimen source and biofilm strength (p = 0.011), with sputum isolates showing the highest moderate biofilm formation (75%). However, no significant association was observed between biofilm phenotype and antibiotic resistance. The coexistence of MDR-associated genes and biofilm-forming ability underscores P. aeruginosa as a critical MDR pathogen. The high prevalence ofGES and parC, combined with the association between respiratory origin and moderate biofilm formation, highlights its adaptive success. Continuous surveillance, antimicrobial stewardship, routine colistin MIC testing, and anti-biofilm therapeutic approaches are essential to mitigate the clinical impact of MDR P. aeruginosa infections.

title: Detection of blaVIM, blaIMP, blaNDM, blaKPC and blaOXA-48-like carbapenemase genes in carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales clinical isolates with phenotypic and genotypic antimicrobial susceptibility to colistin
abstract: Carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales (CRE) are WHO critical-priority pathogens, and detection of carbapenemase production and mcr-1-mediated colistin resistance is important for guiding therapy and preventing antimicrobial resistance spread. In this prospective cross-sectional study, a total of 144 non-duplicate CRE clinical isolates were subjected to the Modified Carbapenem Inactivation Method (mCIM) ± EDTA-modified Carbapenem Inactivation Method (eCIM) test, followed by in-house (laboratory-developed) conventional multiplex polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for simultaneous detection of five common carbapenemase genes, viz. blaVIM, blaIMP, blaNDM, blaKPC and blaOXA-48-like genes. Colistin susceptibility was performed by the broth microdilution method, followed by in-house (laboratory-developed) conventional PCR to detect mcr-1 gene. 73.6% (106/144) of CRE isolates were positive for mCIM test, i.e., CP-CRE, while 96% (102/106) of them were positive for eCIM test. Among eCIM positive CRE (i.e., Metallo-β-lactamase producers), 56% (57/102) were positive for blaNDM gene, 9.8% (10/102) were positive for blaVIM gene, and 2.9% (3/102) were positive for blaIMP gene. Among eCIM negative mCIM positive CRE (i.e., Serine ± Metallo-β-lactamase producers), all four were positive for blaOXA-48-like gene. Colistin had intermediate susceptibility of 90.3% (130/144). mcr-1 gene was detected in five isolates i.e., three with colistin resistant isolates (21.4%; 3/14) and two in colistin intermediate cases with MIC 1 and 2 µg/mL each. Majority of CRE in Indian settings were CP-CRE, with predominance of Metallo-β-lactamase producers (MBL-CRE). blaNDM gene was the most common carbapenemase gene. Colistin resistance (9.7%) was spreading fast, with the mcr-1 gene (21.4%) being a significant contributor.

title: Stage-Resolved Dynamics of Antibiotic Resistance Genes and Mobile Genetic Elements in Full-Scale Anaerobic Digestion Systems
abstract: Anaerobic digestion (AD) has the potential to reduce antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) and mobile genetic elements (MGEs) during waste treatment, yet evidence from full-scale systems remains limited. In particular, process-stage dynamics and host-associated resistance mechanisms are poorly understood, and the relative importance of operational and physicochemical drivers remains unresolved. Here, we profiled process-oriented, stage-resolved resistome and mobilome dynamics across substrates, digestates, and storages from ten farm-scale AD plants, resolving putative host-ARG-MGE coabundance associations across sequential process stages. An integrated framework combining high-throughput qPCR and 16S rRNA gene sequencing was used to quantify ARG and MGE dynamics and characterize microbial community structure. Across different AD systems, ARGs and MGEs exhibited heterogeneous abundance changes, with no consistent patterns. However, elevated pH and NH3 were associated with decreasing trends but were not solely determinative. Stage-resolved correlation networks revealed that ARG-MGE associations formed a conserved structural backbone, whereas putative host associations underwent continuous reshuffling across process stages. This indicates that resistance persistence is driven less by stable taxon associations and more by the redistribution of ARG-MGE units among microbial taxa. Collectively, these results demonstrate that stage-resolved, network-informed analyses provide an informative framework for evaluating resistance persistence and potential environmental risks associated with digestate application.

title: Longitudinal Multiomics Reveals Core Microbiome Disruption and Potential Keystone-Associated Recovery Following Pesticide Exposure
abstract: Pesticides have become indispensable in modern agriculture, serving as a primary tool to minimize crop loss amid increasing human population pressures. While the negative effects of pesticides on the soil microbiome have been reported, the temporal dynamics of soil microorganisms under pesticide use remain underexplored. Specifically, limited knowledge exists regarding how the soil microbiome responds to pesticides before and after the manufacturer-labeled 'safe period' of 21 days after application. We conducted a longitudinal microcosm study to investigate the temporal impacts of herbicide, fungicide, and insecticide on soil microbial diversity, composition, network complexity, and functional pathways across five time points. Our results show that soil microbial communities are negatively impacted by pesticide applications, but there is a trend of recovery after 21 days. We found a significant impact of the temporal persistence of pesticides on both bacterial and fungal community composition, with a stronger effect on fungi. Network analysis revealed that core microbiome networks were negatively impacted by pesticide applications, with the core microbial nodes, raw associations, and modularity declining in pesticide-treated soils, and this negative effect was particularly strong for pyrethroid insecticides. We identified several differentially abundant taxa, including Xanthobacteraceae and Vicinamibacteriales among bacteria, and Mortierella, Mytilinidales among fungi, which could serve as useful biomarkers for pesticide-affected soils. Results from microbial co-occurrence network analysis revealed that one ASV assigned to the Methyloligellaceae family consistently emerged as a keystone taxon in pesticide-treated soils. Using genome-resolved metagenomics, we assembled the genomes (MAGs) of Methyloligellaceae members and found these taxa harbor putative genes associated with pesticide degradation and antimicrobial resistance, suggesting their possible role in community recovery. Given the remarkably dynamic nature of soil microbial communities, our findings bridge an important knowledge gap regarding the short-term dynamics of microbial structures and functional pathways in response to major pesticides.

title: Phage-Based Biofilm Control in Engineered Water Environments
abstract: Biofilms represent a predominant bacterial lifestyle and contribute to the ecological stability and biochemical functioning in water systems. Paradoxically, excessive biofilm formation threatens water security and public health by causing biofouling, harboring pathogens, and facilitating the transmission of antimicrobial resistance. Phage treatment offers a promising strategy for the targeted regulation of biofilm microecology without generating harmful disinfection byproducts. However, its performance in environmental settings can be constrained by spatiotemporal heterogeneity, suboptimal phage exposure, and the evolution of phage resistance in bacteria, creating additional challenges for engineering applications. Here, we synthesize phage-based biofilm control as a multilevel intervention paradigm organized by biological bottlenecks. We examine strategies that improve transport and host access, enhance targeting and productive lysis, induce biofilm disruption through prophage activation, and perturb biofilm communities through keystone-centered interactions. We then align these intervention principles with distinct biofilm scenarios and operational constraints in engineered water environments. Emerging technologies are evaluated according to their roles in target identification, validation under application-relevant conditions, and treatment monitoring. Finally, we propose a closed-loop framework encompassing system diagnosis, intervention design and validation, monitored deployment, and adaptive management. Overall, this Review provides an integrated roadmap for advancing scalable and sustainable phage-based biofilm control in engineered water environments.

title: Outer Membrane Vesicles as a Potential Pathway for Antibiotic Resistance Transfer between Cyanobacteria and Bacteria
abstract: Antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) have profoundly exacerbated environmental risks to public health, evolving into a pressing ecological dilemma. Distinct from traditional pathways, outer membrane vesicles (OMVs) are emerging as important vectors for horizontal gene transfer (HGT) in aquatic environments, yet their role in inter-phylum ARG dissemination remains unclear. In this study, we demonstrate that OMVs mediate bidirectional HGT of ARGs between the cyanobacterium Synechocystis sp. PCC 6803 and Escherichia coli DH5α. Co-incubation experiments confirmed that OMVs derived from either strain could associate with the other, accompanied by successful functional expression of transferred resistance genes. In simulated aquatic environmental conditions, OMVs supplementation increased HGT frequency by 1.49-2.27 folds compared to the control group on day 5. Metagenomic analysis further revealed that OMVs carrying resistance genes induced subtle shifts in coastal microbial community composition. Our findings establish OMVs as mobile genetic packages that enable ARGs exchange between cyanobacteria and heterotrophic bacteria, highlighting a previously overlooked pathway for environmental dissemination of ARGs and providing a theoretical basis for mitigating antibiotic resistance risks in aquatic ecosystems.

title: One Health phylogenomics of antibiotic-resistant Salmonella enterica reveals cross-source relatedness and detection of mcr-3-carrying ST34 isolates in Hong Kong
abstract: Nontyphoidalserovars are a major driver of foodborne illnesses in Hong Kong. Beyond well-recognized extended spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL)- and carbapenemase-producing strains, colistin resistance remains a critical concern for treating severe multidrug-resistant (MDR) infections. While routine surveillance exists, the distribution and genomic epidemiology of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) across interconnected reservoirs remain insufficiently characterized. Applying a One Health framework, this study investigated cross-sectoral genetic relatedness and shared AMR determinants by analyzing local clinical and retail meatisolates alongside a reference set of publicly available regional genomes representing human, food, animal, and environmental sectors. We report the detection of-positive. Typhimurium ST34 lineage human clinical isolates in Hong Kong, includingand, not previously detected in our regional dataset or local genomic surveillance archives. Nanopore sequencing revealed thatwas carried on a mosaic IncC/IncFII plasmid displaying structural features consistent with a recombinant origin involving genetic elements shared between clinicaland chicken-derivedplasmid backbones. These plasmids demonstrated hightransferability to diverse Enterobacterales, including,andspp. Additionally, identification of a transferable--carrying plasmid from a pork-derived isolate highlights the presence andmobility of clinically important carbapenenemase determinants within food-derived strains. Comparative phylogenomic analysis of 1,458genomes identified mixed-source genomic clusters among major sequence types (ST19, ST34, ST155, ST40, ST17, and ST2529), indicating genomic relatedness across multiple One Health sectors. These findings support the utility of integrated One Health genomic surveillance frameworks to monitor multidrug-resistantlineages.

title: Soil antibiotic resistance genes at the One Health interface: Evidence trajectories, dissemination risks, and risk-based management
abstract: Soils serve as reservoirs and transmission interfaces for antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs), which can function as mobile genetic contaminants by persisting and replicating within microbial hosts and propagating via horizontal gene transfer (HGT). However, evidence linking mitigation mechanisms to environmental risk reduction remains insufficiently synthesized. Here, we integrate bibliometric trajectory analysis with mechanistic synthesis, using 2,309 Web of Science Core Collection records published between 2008 and 2026 to identify research trajectories, knowledge structures, and emerging mitigation fronts. The field has shifted from occurrence surveys and source identification toward intervention-oriented control, accelerating markedly after 2019. Foundational knowledge centers on soil resistome dynamics, mobile genetic element (MGE)-mediated HGT, and contaminant-driven co-selection. Current fronts highlight biochar-mediated regulation, manure and compost management, reactive oxygen species (ROS)-driven or photocatalytic inactivation of extracellular deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA), and ARG responses under co-contamination by antibiotics, heavy metals, and microplastics. Beyond mapping research trends, this review constructs a three-tier mitigation framework spanning extracellular DNA deconstruction and sequestration, MGE-mediated transfer inhibition, and system-level microecological restructuring through source management and soil amendment. Future work should integrate absolute gene loads, host identity, ARG-MGE linkage, transfer frequency, soil biogeochemical context, and field-scale ecological rebound into mechanistically grounded and ecologically defensible evaluation frameworks that assess reductions in ARG dissemination risk alongside effects on soil function, ecological resilience, and organic resource circularity.

title: Hybrid genome assemblies of Bacteroidota isolates uncover mobile genetic elements, antimicrobial resistance genes, and novel antimicrobial peptides
abstract: Members of the phylumdominate the mammalian gut microbiota and represent promising candidates for next-generation probiotics. However, the resolution of completegenomes is often hindered by extensive repetitive sequences and mobile genetic elements, a technical challenge further exacerbated by high intraspecies diversity and strain-level variants that drive assembly fragmentation and preclude the recovery of contiguous scaffolds. We recently isolated 18 strains that belonged to theorder offrom mouse ceca, human feces, and tortoise stool, which we now sequenced using both Illumina and Oxford Nanopore platforms. We developed a specialized assembly workflow to reconstruct high-resolution genomes and characterize their extrachromosomal landscapes. The hybrid pipeline yielded 2 fully closed, single-contig chromosomes, 10 almost closed genomes, and 6 draft assemblies. Genomic integrity was exceptionally high, with completeness scores ranging from 99.6% to 100% and contamination levels below 2%. A total of 12 circular plasmids were detected across 10 isolates; eight isolates harbored a single plasmid, while two isolates (241163E and 241171E) each carried two distinct circular plasmids. Seven of these plasmids were experimentally confirmed through isolation and sequencing, and five were classified as viral contigs. Functional annotation revealed a diverse repertoire of antimicrobial resistance genes and identified several predicted antimicrobial peptides in the assemblies through machine-learning analysis, of which two selected ones were experimentally verified. Overall, the resulting assemblies provide a reliable foundation for tracking mobile genetic elements, assessing resistance potential, and mining bioactive peptides inspecies intended for therapeutic development. Bacteria in the phylumare essential to mammalian gut health and are currently being developed as advanced probiotics. However, their complex DNA often prevents scientists from mapping their complete genetic blueprints, which can leave hidden traits like antibiotic resistance undetected. In this study, we combined two advanced DNA sequencing methods to create highly accurate and complete genetic maps for 18isolates from humans, mice, and tortoise. We successfully uncovered small, elusive DNA rings (potential plasmids) and confirmed their physical presence in the laboratory. Furthermore, we identified genes responsible for antibiotic resistance and used artificial intelligence to discover new antimicrobial peptides. This research provides a crucial foundation for the scientific community to accurately track mobile genes, rigorously evaluate the safety of potential gut therapeutics, and discover novel molecules for medical applications.

title: Stimuli-Responsive Copper Modified Mesoporous Silica Nanoparticles as Smart Antimicrobial Delivery System for Antimicrobial Applications
abstract: The emergence of multidrug-resistant pathogens poses a significant challenge to conventional antimicrobial therapies and underscores the urgent need for innovative therapeutic strategies using highly efficacious and less toxic antimicrobial compounds, as well as more targeted antimicrobial delivery strategies to prevent uncontrolled release, which contributes to the rise of drug resistance. In this study, the design and synthesis of copper-modified mesoporous silica nanoparticles (Cu-MSNs) were described as a stimuli-responsive, smart antimicrobial delivery system incorporating carvacrol as a bioactive alternative to conventional antibiotics. The Cu-MSNs exhibit high surface area, tunable pore size, and efficient carvacrol loading. Copper ions embedded within the silica matrix provide intrinsic antimicrobial activity and may enhance the antimicrobial effect of carvacrol. Poly(2-(dimethylamino) ethyl methacrylate) (PDMAEMA) brushes were anchored on Cu-MSNs via surface-initiated atom transfer radical polymerization (SI-ATRP). The PDMAEMA brushes provided stimuli-responsive behavior, enabling pH- and temperature-dependent modulation of carvacrol release. The successful synthesis of Cu-MSN-PDMAEMA has been confirmed by Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), elemental analysis (EA), and transmission electron microscopy (TEM). Moreover, stimuli-responsive behavior was confirmed using dynamic light scattering (DLS) experiments, demonstrating the pH- and temperature-dependent response of the PDMAEMA brushes. Finally, the carvacrol release behavior was studied at different pH values by using a sensitive paper-based electrochemical sensor. The multifunctional nanoplatform exhibited antimicrobial activity against both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria as well as antiviral activity against representative enveloped and non-enveloped viral models. This synergistic design combines the benefits of a natural antimicrobial agent, intrinsic metallic activity, and smart polymer regulation, offering an strategy to enhance efficacy while minimizing off-target effects. Release studies demonstrated pH-triggered carvacrol delivery, with enhanced release under acidic conditions, confirming the gating function of the PDMAEMA brushes, highlighting the potential of these particles as an antibiotic-free alternative for preventing microbial infections while mitigating the development of antimicrobial resistance (AMR).

title: Adjunctive Use of Azithromycin to Non-Surgical Periodontal Therapy: Rationale and Evidence for Its Use in Periodontitis-A Scoping Review
abstract: Antimicrobials are added as adjuncts to non-surgical periodontal therapy in certain cases to achieve improved outcomes. Among the adjunct antimicrobials that have gained renewed interest is azithromycin, owing to its additional anti-inflammatory and host-modulating properties. This review aims to summarise the pharmacology, adverse effects, and the current evidence for the adjunct use of azithromycin in different forms of periodontitis. In vitro studies, randomized controlled trials, and longitudinal studies published in English were searched in MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science and Google Scholar (https://osf.io/m8enj/overview). Following screening of 677 articles, 70 articles were subjected to full-text review and ultimately 57 articles were included. In vitro studies demonstrated anti-bacterial, host-modulating, and anti-inflammatory properties of azithromycin with drug concentrating in inflamed tissues. The additional benefits of adjunctive azithromycin are moderate and inconsistent, although deep periodontal pockets may show enhanced improvements. Local delivery of azithromycin demonstrated additional benefits in single-rooted teeth. Azithromycin may provide clinical and microbiological benefits, especially in deep periodontal pockets. However, the World Health Organization categorizes azithromycin as a critically important antimicrobial for human medicine. Due to inconsistent results and owing to the importance of azithromycin, the adjunctive use of azithromycin with non-surgical periodontal therapy is currently not recommended.

title: gcPathogen 2.0: an expanded multi-omics database advancing global pathogen surveillance and One Health research
abstract: Launched in 2024, gcPathogen established a critical foundation for the genomic surveillance of human pathogens. Here, we present gcPathogen 2.0, a major multi-omics update designed to address key analytical bottlenecks, including the integration of genomic and transcriptional profiles, systematic tracking of cross-habitat distribution, and large-scale discovery of antimicrobial peptides (AMPs). This release expands coverage from 1134 to 1506 pathogenic species, spanning 557 bacteria, 508 fungi, 258 viruses, and 183 parasites, and increases total genomic records past 2.3 million. By incorporating 12 597 transcriptomes across 148 species, gcPathogen 2.0 bridges the gap between gene carriage and functional expression for risk assessment. Furthermore, the platform integrates 285 925 pathogen metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) spanning human, animal, and environmental niches. Mapped across 68 Environment Ontology (ENVO) habitat categories, these MAGs enable comprehensive tracking of cross-habitat distribution of pathogens, antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs), virulence factors (VFs), and mobile genetic elements (MGEs). Leveraging a nonredundant reference set curated from seven public databases, we identified over 77 million AMPs belonging to >55 000 families across 438 bacterial pathogens. Finally, pan-genome analyses of 440 bacterial species map intraspecies functional distributions across core, accessory, and unique gene repertoires. gcPathogen 2.0 is publicly accessible at https://nmdc.cn/gcpathogen/.

title: Redox-triggered electronic modulation and ligand dissociation in cobalt(iii) bipyridine prodrugs for urease inhibition in Helicobacter pylori
abstract: infection is one of the most significant health problems on a global scale, and the treatment has become, more than ever, less effective due to antibiotic resistance and low drug specificity. This work describes a redox-responsive cobalt-based prodrug system to specifically deliver acetohydroxamic acid (AHA) to urease for its inhibition. A cobalt(iii)-bipyridine coordination complex was designed to stabilize AHA during its systemic delivery and release it under reductive conditions typical of the infected gastric microenvironment. Density functional theory computations show that the oxidized Co(iii) form is strongly bonded to the metal, and structurally, the form is kinetically stable, but reduction to Co(ii) causes elongation of the bonds and a marked reduction in ligand-exchange energy. Molecular docking and replicated molecular dynamics simulations, comprising a total of 3.3 µs of production dynamics acrossurease, a comparativeurease model, and human carbonic anhydrase I, are used to evaluate target-site access and off-target metal accessibility. Across both urease systems, free AHA remains metal-proximal, while the intact cobalt cage shows restricted access to the dinuclear nickel center. A human carbonic-anhydrase I comparison similarly supports reduced direct metal access by the intact prodrug. The redox potential, activation energetics, and lipophilicity of the bipyridine ligand can be systematically tuned by the substituent modification of the ligand. Altogether, we create a defined, tunable platform to design redox-activated antimicrobial prodrugs, connecting coordination chemistry and targeted therapeutic activation for future applications.

title: Glucose-Fueled Gold Nanozymes Achieve Picomolar Eradication of Drug-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) represents a worsening global health emergency, with projections estimating more than 39 million deaths attributable to drug-resistant bacteria by 2050. Diabetic patients face a compounded threat: chronic hyperglycemia suppresses host immunity while enriching wound microenvironments with glucose, accelerating methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) proliferation and rendering conventional antibiotics increasingly ineffective. Here, we report a minimalist, enzyme-free antibacterial strategy based on citrate-stabilized 30 nm gold nanoparticles (AuNPs) that exploit this glucose surplus as a catalytic substrate. Through intrinsic glucose oxidase- and peroxidase-like dual activities, these AuNPs convert ambient glucose and oxygen into a localized cascade of bactericidal reactive oxygen species (ROS), achieving >90% growth inhibition against both methicillin-susceptible S. aureus (MSSA) and MRSA USA300 at concentrations as low as 12.5 pM. Scavenger experiments establish oxidative membrane damage as the primary killing mechanism, and SEM and TEM analyses confirm that AuNPs preferentially accumulate at the bacterial cell membrane, confining ROS production to the site of maximum biological vulnerability. This membrane-localized catalysis, further amplified by brief 532 nm irradiation, accounts for the marked superiority of spherical AuNPs over gold nanorods of comparable composition, demonstrating that spatial localization rather than bulk ROS output governs the killing efficiency. This glucose-fueled, antibiotic-free platform offers a rational strategy for treating drug-resistant infections in hyperglycemic wound environments.

title: Receptor-Targeted Sequential Phage Dosing against Pseudomonas aeruginosa PAO1: An In Vitro Proof-of-Concept Study
abstract: Antibiotic resistance has intensified the need for alternative therapies, such as bacteriophage administration. However, the optimal delivery strategy-specifically simultaneous versus sequential dosing-remains poorly defined for ensuring sustainable efficacy. This single-strain, in vitro proof-of-concept study evaluated receptor-targeted sequential dosing using phages Dobby, targeting lipopolysaccharide, and MPK7, targeting type IV pili, against P. aeruginosa PAO1. Time-kill assays were conducted at various multiplicities of infection (MOI: 0.01, 1, and 100) to compare simultaneous and sequential dosing regimens.
