Resistance profiling was performed to assess the fitness costs of resulting isolates, while atomic force microscopy infrared spectroscopy (AFM-IR) was utilized to identify chemical signatures and underlying resistance mechanisms in phage-resistant mutants. Sequential treatment, particularly initiating therapy with the LPS-specific phage Dobby followed by MPK7, was more effective than simultaneous dosing, achieving bacterial reductions exceeding 3-log10 within 48 h. Notably, low MOI (0.01) sequential treatments maintained sustained population suppression, whereas high MOI (100) treatments triggered rapid bacterial rebound. Resistance profiling confirmed that Dobby-resistant isolates exhibited lower fitness costs, rendering them more susceptible to subsequent MPK7 treatment. AFM-IR revealed unique chemical alterations in resistant mutants, specifically linked to LPS truncation and TFP dysfunction. In the Dobby-MPK7-PAO1 model, receptor-specific sequential dosing produced more sustained bacterial suppression than simultaneous treatment. This proof-of-concept supports further evaluation of temporal phage dosing across diverse P. aeruginosa strains and phage combinations.

title: Clinicobacteriological profile, Mortality Predictors and Antimicrobial Resistance in Necrotising Soft Tissue Infections: A prospective study
abstract: Necrotising soft tissue infections (NSTIs) are rapidly progressive infections requiring prompt diagnosis and management. This study assessed predictors of mortality, microbiological spectrum, antimicrobial resistance patterns, and differences between polymicrobial and monomicrobial NSTIs in a prospective manner. This study enrolled patients aged 15 years or older with clinically suspected NSTIs who presented between March 2022 and February 2023. Clinical, laboratory, surgical, and outcome data were collected. Tissue and pus samples were processed for aerobic and anaerobic cultures. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing was performed according to CLSI guidelines. Mortality-associated factors were analysed using univariate analysis, binary logistic regression, and survival analysis. Eighty-seven patients were included, predominantly male (87.3%), with a median age of 47.5 years. Extremities were most commonly affected. The mortality rate of this cohort was 25.3%. Polymicrobial infections predominated (49.4%), while monomicrobial NSTIs were associated with higher mortality (p = 0.022). Gram-negative organisms, particularly Acinetobacter baumannii and Escherichia coli, were the most frequent pathogens. Obligate anaerobes were significantly associated with polymicrobial infections. Chronic liver disease (p = 0.003) and systemic toxicity (p = 0.018) independently predicted mortality, whereas higher haemoglobin levels were protective. High antimicrobial resistance was observed, including carbapenem-resistant A. baumannii and Enterobacterales. Among the anaerobes, resistance to clindamycin and cefoxitin, along with reduced susceptibility to metronidazole, was reported. NSTIs remain associated with substantial mortality, especially in monomicrobial infections due to multidrug-resistant Gram-negative pathogens. Early recognition, prompt surgery, and region-specific empirical antimicrobial therapy are crucial for improving outcomes.

title: Morphology-dependent Fe3O4 nanozymes with NIR-enhanced peroxidase-like activity for antibacterial wound therapy
abstract: Bacterial infection severely impairs wound repair, and antibiotic-based treatment is increasingly challenged by antimicrobial resistance. Herein, Fe3O4 nanozymes with octahedral, spherical, and cubic morphologies were synthesized and systematically compared for peroxidase-like activity, photothermal performance, and antibacterial efficacy. Despite their comparable sizes and good dispersibility, the three nanozymes exhibited distinct morphology-dependent catalytic activities. Octahedral Fe3O4 nanoparticles (O-IONP) showed the highest POD-like activity, strongest hydroxyl radical generation, lowest apparent Michaelis constant toward TMB, and highest maximum reaction velocity. The catalytic activity of Fe3O4 nanozymes increased with temperature and reached an optimum near 55 oC, indicating the feasibility of photothermalenhanced catalysis. Under 808 nm near-infrared irradiation, O-IONP displayed the most efficient photothermal response and reached a temperature favourable for POD-like catalysis. In vitro, O-IONP combined with NIR reduced Escherichia coli viability to approximately 2% and caused severe bacterial membrane deformation, collapse, and rupture, while maintaining acceptable cytocompatibility toward macrophages. In an E. coli-infected wound model, O-IONP with NIR significantly accelerated wound closure, reducing the wound remaining ratio to approximately 13% on day 10. This work demonstrates a simple morphology-engineered Fe3O4 nanozyme platform for photothermal-catalytic antibacterial therapy and infected wound healing.

title: Erdosteine Enhances Tobramycin Activity Against a Tobramycin-Resistant Clinical Isolate and PAO1 Reference Strain of Pseudomonas aeruginosa
abstract: Chronic respiratory infections caused by pathogens including Pseudomonas aeruginosa (P. aeruginosa) pose a major therapeutic challenge in patients with pulmonary diseases such as cystic fibrosis (CF) and non-CF bronchiectasis, where treatment efficacy is limited by the formation of biofilms, the emergence of multidrug resistant pathogens and a shortage of new and effective antibiotic classes. One approach to address this problem involves the use of "antibiotic enhancers", which are compounds that potentiate the activity of existing antibiotics without possessing direct antimicrobial effects of their own. The mucoactive thiol-based prodrug erdosteine, currently approved for the treatment of acute and chronic respiratory diseases, has been reported to exhibit anti-adhesive activity against respiratory pathogens, suggesting a clinically relevant contribution to the prevention of bacterial colonisation. Furthermore, in addition to reported anti-inflammatory and antioxidant activities, erdosteine has demonstrated the ability to potentiate the activity of various antimicrobial drugs. However, to date, whether erdosteine can enhance the activity of tobramycin, an antibiotic widely used to treat pathogens in the respiratory tract, has not been investigated. In this study, we investigated the ability of MET-1, the primary active metabolite of erdosteine, to enhance the activity of tobramycin against P. aeruginosa strains using a panel of both in vitro and in vivo assays. The activity of both mono- and combination therapies was measured in planktonic P. aeruginosa (strains RP73 & PAO1) using in vitro microdilution assays including chequerboard analysis and time-kill assays, whilst activity against biofilms were analysed using microtiter plate assays with readouts including total biomass, metabolic activity, and bacterial enumeration. Combination therapy of 40 mg/kg tobramycin and 100 mg/kg erdosteine was also assessed in vivo using a murine model of chronic pulmonary infection induced by P. aeruginosa. 10 mg/L MET-1 significantly enhanced the antimicrobial activity of tobramycin in planktonic cultures of RP73 at 24 h and PAO1 at 4 h, leading to a greater than 2 logreduction in bacterial numbers compared to tobramycin monotherapy, despite MET-1 demonstrating no intrinsic bactericidal activity. In mature biofilms, MET-1 substantially enhanced tobramycin activity, reducing the biomass-derived IC₅₀ by approximately 18-fold in RP73 and 13-fold in PAO1. Finally, combination therapy of 40 mg/kg tobramycin and 100 mg/kg erdosteine was associated with a lower pulmonary bacterial burden in a murine model of chronic pulmonary infection. Our in vitro and in vivo studies highlight the ability of erdosteine to potentiate the activity of tobramycin suggesting that erdosteine has the potential to reduce the burden of long-term antimicrobial therapies in patients with chronic respiratory infections and thus improve clinical outcomes.

title: Reducing bacterial resistance evolution through antimicrobial peptide modifications
abstract: Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) have emerged as promising alternatives to conventional antibiotics, yet bacteria can evolve resistance toward them through mechanisms that are poorly understood. Here, we selected a well-characterized antimicrobial peptide, melittin, as a model peptide that was shown to induce high levels of resistance in the human pathogen. We hypothesize that the physicochemical properties of AMPs might play a role in resistance development. To explore this hypothesis, we used computational approaches to design melittin derivatives with diverse physicochemical characteristics. A data set of 191 melittin-derived sequences (8-26 amino acids long) was analyzed to identify representative peptides spanning diverse physicochemical clusters. Selected peptides were synthesized and tested in an experimental evolution assay. Resistance dynamics, cross-resistance patterns, and cytotoxicity were evaluated in parallel. Full-length melittin with an amide or carboxylic acid C' terminus and highly hydrophobic derivatives [e.g., Mel(2-22)] showed high resistance occurrence, whereas Mel(5-24), a truncated variant, maintained antimicrobial activity while eliciting minimal resistance development. Whole-genome sequencing of endpoint populations revealed that melittin-evolved strains accumulated convergent mutations most prominently in, whereas Mel(5-24)-evolved populations converged only on, with no mutations in canonical resistance loci, suggesting fewer accessible adaptive pathways against the truncated peptide. Our results indicate that peptide hydrophobicity and chain length correlated with resistance fold change, whereas coil propensity showed a negative correlation. Notably, Mel(5-24) displayed reduced cross-resistance to other peptides and lower cytotoxicity toward mammalian cells than melittin, suggesting a broader therapeutic window. Overall, our findings indicate that tuning peptide hydrophobicity and chain length along with structural propensity can mitigate the evolutionary pressure driving resistance while maintaining antibacterial potency. Rational modulation of such physicochemical properties may provide a practical route for designing AMPs with improved selectivity and lower resistance potential.

title: Mining and engineering novel staphylococcal lysostaphins as species-specific antibacterial agents
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) presents a serious global healthcare challenge, with staphylococci, especially, being the main cause of deadly infections. Peptidoglycan hydrolases, particularly lysostaphins, are highly promising alternatives to traditional antibiotics, collectively termed enzybiotics, due to their specific lytic action against the bacterial cell wall. To thoroughly explore their therapeutic potential, we performed comprehensive genome mining of 118,127 staphylococcal and 500 closely related mammaliicoccal genomes. Ultimately, we discovered 19 unique lysostaphin sequences, divided into four distinct evolutionary clusters. By characterizing five novel lysostaphins alongside known references, we observed diverse lytic activities and species-specificities. Notably, we identified a novel lysostaphin variant from, Lys-Ssim, representing a previously unknown evolutionary cluster, which exhibits unmatched substrate promiscuity and an unprecedented lytic activity that extends beyond staphylococci. Additionally, structural modeling and site-directed mutagenesis revealed that peptidoglycan hydrolysis by these M23 metalloproteases depends on highly flexible conformations of the binding cleft. Using these structural insights, we successfully engineered lysostaphins with significantly improved enzyme selectivity forwhile nearly eliminating activity against the skin commensal. We also demonstrated the potential to engineer lysostaphins active against species other than staphylococci. Our findings show that natural staphylococcal lysostaphins are a rich, highly specialized resource for developing rationally engineered, microbiota-friendly antibacterial agents.

title: High-Throughput Synthesis and Screening of Cyclometalated Iridium Complexes for Antibacterial Applications
abstract: The discovery of novel antibiotics to address the rise of antimicrobial resistance is an increasingly pressing issue for global health. In recent years, transition-metal complexes have gained attention as potential antibacterial agents. We herein describe a new methodology to generate novel cyclometalated iridium compounds with bidentate Schiff ligands in a high-throughput combinatorial approach, alongside the expansion of an existing approach using bidentate pyridine-triazole ligands, with the aim of finding new metalloantibiotics. A total of 552 new complexes were synthesized and evaluated. Variety in the libraries was introduced by including three cyclometalating phenylpyridine ligands, demonstrating that the synthesis can tolerate both electron-rich and electron-poor metal scaffolds while using mild and biologically compatible conditions. Screening of the crude reaction mixtures in a direct-to-biology approach revealed a number of highly active complexes against Gram-positive bacteria, which was confirmed by resynthesis and further testing of lead compounds. This approach widens the scope of metal complex combinatorial chemistry, enabling rapid exploration of the chemical space involving cyclometalated iridium complexes.

title: Antimicrobial Peptide Databases and Prediction Tools: Toward a Standard Evaluation Framework
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) has a profound impact on animal and human health and is associated with substantial morbidity, mortality, and public health costs. There is a clear need to develop novel, effective antibiotic agents, which can overcome the current AMR crisis. Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) may offer such a solution and have attracted growing attention for their potential to combat AMR. In parallel, the growing availability of peptide sequences in public databases has stimulated the development of numerous machine learning and deep learning tools to predict antimicrobial activity computationally. However, it remains unclear how reliably these tools can be compared, as existing studies often rely on heterogeneous data sets and inconsistent evaluation protocols that may lead to data leakage and inflated performance estimates. This raises a central question: what evaluation criteria and benchmark resources are needed to enable fair, reproducible, and biologically meaningful assessment of AMP prediction tools? We address this question by focusing specifically on antibacterial peptides (ABPs). We first provide an overview of AMP databases relevant to antibacterial activity and compare their content, redundancy, and experimental metadata. We then critically assess existing computational tools for ABP prediction, highlighting key limitations related to data set construction, affinity to certain sequences, data leakage, and inconsistent performance reporting. Based on these limitations, we propose a reference evaluation framework designed to improve comparability, reproducibility, and practical utility in ABP prediction. Finally, we provide targeted recommendations for AMP databases and future tool development to support more robust progress in the computational discovery of ABPs.

title: A dual endogenous selectable marker system for Aspergillus flavus and its application in characterizing nsdD function in development and aflatoxin biosynthesis
abstract: poses a significant threat to global food security and public health, as it not only triggers severe mold spoilage in staple crops like peanuts and corn but also produces aflatoxin, a potent carcinogen. However, genetic manipulation of this fungus is notoriously challenging due to its inherent insensitivity to conventional antibiotics. To overcome this barrier, we established a robust, fully endogenous genetic transformation system for a highly toxigenic wild-type strain,-SD, using polyethylene glycol (PEG)-mediated protoplast transfection with two selectable markers:(uracil auxotrophy/5-FOA counterselection) and aE198A point mutation (carbendazim resistance). We successfully constructed the tool strains with awhich were used for gene knockout and overexpression, and theE198A mutant was used for gene complementation. To validate the operational efficacy of this platform, we performed knockout, complementation, and overexpression of thegene as a test case. This study provides a reliable technical foundation for elucidating the molecular mechanisms governing aflatoxin biosynthesis and pathogenicity, thereby facilitating the identification of novel targets forcontrol. This study established a novel genetic transformation system for a highly toxigenic wild-type strain,-SD, utilizing fully endogenous selectable markers:(uracil auxotrophy/5-FOA counterselection) and aE198A point mutation (carbendazim resistance). This platform eliminates the need for heterologous antibiotic resistance cassettes, thereby reducing biosafety concerns while enabling iterative genome editing through marker recycling. Using this system, we demonstrated its efficacy by validating the expected phenotypic changes uponmanipulation, revealing a previously unrecognized trade-off between sclerotia formation and aflatoxin biosynthesis. This work provides a valuable, compliance-friendly resource for the fungal research community and lays a foundation for identifying novel targets to disrupt fungal persistence and mycotoxin production in agricultural settings.

title: Draft genome sequences of two Stenotrophomonas muris isolates, CBAS 1154 and CBAS 1234, recovered from patients with ICU-acquired ventilator-associated sepsis
abstract: We report the high-quality draft genome sequences of two clinicalisolates recovered from the lower respiratory tract of intensive care unit patients with ventilator-associated sepsis in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. Based on our review of the available literature, we found no previous records of this species from Brazil.

title: Postmortem pulmonary concentrations of tilmicosin and gamithromycin in cattle with fatal bovine respiratory disease
abstract: Bovine respiratory disease (BRD) is a health and economic problem in intensive beef production. Antimicrobial (ATM) therapy requires adequate ATM concentrations at the pulmonary infection site. This study determined pulmonary concentrations of tilmicosin (TIL) and gamithromycin (GAM) in cattle that died from BRD under field conditions and characterized the ATM susceptibility of isolates recovered from affected lungs. Lung samples from 41 cattle were analyzed by liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry. TIL was detected in 56.1% of lungs (0.013-8.811 µg/g; mean 0.956 µg/g; median 0.117 µg/g), and GAM in 24.4% (0.032-2.323 µg/g; mean 0.570 µg/g; median 0.193 µg/g). Detection of TIL and GAM was significantly associated with reported treatment (p<0.001); in animals with documented treatment, TIL and GAM were detected in 90% and 100% of cases, respectively. Concentrations varied widely between animals and were lower than those previously reported in healthy cattle. This may point to altered pulmonary ATM accumulation in advanced BRD; however, the observational design, without a healthy or survivor comparison group or paired plasma measurements, does not allow this explanation to be established. Susceptibility testing of 46 evaluable isolates showed 93.5% and 97.8% susceptibility to TIL and GAM, respectively. Despite this susceptibility, the animals died; the data cannot establish the cause, which may involve disease stage at treatment, timing of diagnosis, irreversible lung injury, pathogen interactions, host factors, or altered pulmonary ATM distribution. The findings emphasize the need to integrate knowledge of pulmonary ATM distribution, early diagnosis, and rational ATM use to improve BRD outcomes.

title: Sporadic leprosy cases in Europe: a reminder of global health interconnections in the era of travel and migration
abstract: After decades of near absence, the identification of sporadic leprosy (Hansen's disease) cases in Europe has renewed attention to the vulnerability of non-endemic regions to neglected infectious diseases in an era of intensified global mobility. This perspective does not aim to provide a comprehensive quantitative analysis of European case numbers, but rather to interpret the epidemiological significance of isolated cases detected in post-elimination settings. In late 2024 and 2025, individual cases were reported in Romania and Croatia, representing the first documented diagnoses in these countries in several decades. Available epidemiological evidence indicates that these cases were imported, linked to exposure in endemic regions, and not associated with sustained local transmission. Although limited in number, such events remain epidemiologically meaningful given the long and variable incubation period of, the insidious and often paucisymptomatic onset of disease, and declining clinical familiarity in non-endemic contexts. These factors may contribute to delayed recognition and underestimation of true occurrence. Drawing on recent European case reports and existing epidemiological evidence, we argue that imported cases should be interpreted not as isolated anomalies, but as signals of global interconnectedness shaped by travel, labor mobility, and migration. We highlight the importance of maintaining diagnostic awareness, specialized referral pathways, and access to reference laboratory expertise, including molecular tools for antimicrobial resistance surveillance. While the risk of sustained transmission in Europe remains extremely low, continued vigilance is essential, as regional elimination does not equate to global eradication.

title: "Nano-in-Gel Platforms for the Topical Treatment of Staphylococcus aureus Skin Infections"
abstract: Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus) is the leading cause of skin infections worldwide. Rising antimicrobial resistance limits the effectiveness of current treatments, highlighting the need for new therapeutic strategies. In this context, Rifabutin (RFB), could be repurposed for skin infections based on its strong anti-staphylococcal activity. However, its low oral bioavailability, and the rapid capacity of bacteria to develop drug tolerance, makes necessary to find novel platforms to ensure antimicrobial efficacy. This work proposes the development of Nano-in-Gel drug delivery systems, integrating RFB-loaded nanostructured lipid carriers (NLCs) into gelatin hydrogels for topical administration. These composite materials combine the controlled release capacity of hydrogels with NLCs´ ability to maximize RFB clinical potential. RFB-loaded NLCs were prepared and characterized in terms of physicochemical properties and cytocompatibility in human dermal fibroblasts (HDF). Moreover, their antibacterial activity against two different S. aureus strains-including mutants generated after RFB exposure was evaluated using a combination of conventional quantification methods and droplet digital PCR (ddPCR). Following the incorporation of NLCs into the gels, the mechanical properties of the Nano-in-Gel systems, and their ability to modulate nanoparticle release were assessed. Results demonstrated that the RFB-loaded NLCs possessed optimal physicochemical characteristics and high biocompatibility. Furthermore, the nanocarriers exhibited enhanced anti-staphylococcal activity compared to the free drug and successfully overcame RFB-resistance in mutant strains. The Nano-in-Gel platforms showed excellent mechanical performance for topical application and achieved a controlled NLCs release profile. These findings suggest that the Nano-in-Gel systems constitute a promising strategy for the advanced management of S. aureus skin infections.

title: Physiological and ecological drivers of antibiotic resistance selection in microbial communities
abstract: Resistance selection is increasingly recognized as a risk-relevant endpoint for evaluating low-level environmental antibiotic exposure. Although previous studies have shown that microbial community context can substantially alter the minimum selective concentration (MSC), quantitative frameworks that integrate pharmacodynamic traits with ecological interactions remain limited. Here, we developed the MSC-incorporated Simulation of Community-level Outcomes of Pharmacodynamics and Ecology (MSCOPE) model to quantify resistance selection under multispecies interactions. The effects of key physiological parameters (minimum inhibitory concentration, MIC; Hill coefficient, K) and ecological parameters (community diversity, H; interspecific competition, γ) on community-level MSC were then examined using the model. Model simulations indicated that greater effective tolerance of sensitive subpopulations, higher community diversity, and stronger interspecific competition were associated with higher model-derived MSCs, with nonlinear joint effects among physiological and ecological parameters. These patterns were then examined experimentally using synthetic microbial communities (SynComs) assembled from wild-type sensitive Escherichia coli isolates and an engineered kanamycin-resistant E. coli strain, in which aggregate pharmacodynamic traits, within-species strain diversity, and resource availability were systematically varied. Associations between laboratory-derived MSCs and physiological and ecological descriptors were further examined across 16 environmental microbial communities. Overall, MSCOPE provides an integrative modeling and experimental framework for examining how pharmacodynamic traits and ecological context are associated with resistance-selection thresholds and may inform environmental risk assessment of antibiotics.

title: HGSAF: Heterogeneous graph structural alignment and distillation model with attentive fusion for microbe-drug association prediction
abstract: The rapid emergence of antimicrobial resistance necessitates AI-driven computational strategies to navigate the molecular diversity landscape of microbe-drug interactions. While graph neural networks have shown promise in predicting such associations, existing methods struggle with the intertwined challenges of processing topological and semantic features in isolation and handling severe class imbalance inherent in biomedical datasets. In this work, we devised a heterogeneous graph structural alignment and distillation with an attentive fusion model to predict microbe-drug associations. Our model constructs heterogeneous biological graphs alongside meta-path-induced subgraphs to capture complementary views of microbial and drug entities. A layer-adaptive graph transformer is devised to simultaneously encode topological and positional information while mitigating noise and over-smoothing. Critically, we introduce a reciprocal distillation module for dual-path heterogeneous graph learning that mutually transfers structural and semantic knowledge between pathways, eliminating the need for explicit negative sampling during representation alignment. For the final association prediction, unobserved pairs are sampled as negative examples for supervised training, following standard practice. A cross‑graph alignment loss, jointly optimized with focal loss, improves robustness against class imbalance under controlled sampling ratios (1:1 and 1:5). Extensive evaluations, including comparisons against both domain-specialized predictors and general-purpose graph neural network backbones, demonstrate that HGSAF consistently achieves superior performance and highlight the methodological robustness and potential for broader application in biomedical network analysis.

title: Vancomycin presoaking of ligament grafts: State of the Art and graft-specific evidence
abstract: Septic arthritis after ligament reconstruction is uncommon but potentially devastating. Vancomycin graft presoaking was developed as an adjunct to standard systemic prophylaxis and sterile technique to reduce viable Gram-positive contamination before implantation and biofilm maturation. This State-of-the-Art review evaluates its biological rationale, clinical effectiveness, safety, implementation, graft-specific considerations, hypersensitivity, antimicrobial stewardship, geographic variation, cost-effectiveness, and unresolved controversies. A structured narrative search of PubMed was updated through October 11, 2026, supplemented by backward citation screening and targeted review of relevant guidance and evidence syntheses. The clinical evidence remains predominantly observational. Large comparative cohorts and pooled analyses consistently associate vancomycin graft presoaking with lower rates of septic arthritis after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR), with the most direct evidence applying to hamstring autografts. Limited randomized evidence is available but remains underpowered for a rare postoperative infection outcome. Absolute benefit varies with baseline infection risk. Laboratory, animal, and clinical studies have not demonstrated harm within commonly studied short-exposure protocols, although the most direct clinical safety evidence also derives from hamstring autografts. Evidence for bone-patellar tendon-bone grafts, quadriceps tendon grafts, allografts, revision procedures, and non-ACL ligament reconstructions remains substantially more limited or indirect. One uncontrolled 2026 quadriceps tendon series represents an unconfirmed graft-specific safety signal rather than evidence of a contraindication. No alternative graft-presoaking antibiotic currently has a clinical evidence base comparable to vancomycin. Based on the current evidence, vancomycin graft presoaking may be considered as an adjunct to standard systemic prophylaxis in hamstring autograft ACLR within a standardized protocol. It should not replace established infection-prevention measures, and extrapolation to other graft types or reconstruction settings should reflect the directness of the available evidence. Future research should prioritize graft-specific protocol optimization, prospective comparative evidence, antimicrobial-resistance surveillance, and long-term graft and cartilage outcomes.

title: Microbial and antimicrobial resistance signatures differentiate healthy and inflamed ileal pouches in patients with ulcerative colitis
abstract: Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) from healthy donors with a normally functioning colon has limited clinical effect in the treatment of chronic pouchitis. However, a normally functioning ileal pouch-anal anastomosis (IPAA) physiology differs from individuals with a healthy intact colon. We aimed to investigate the microbial characteristics of patients with a normally functioning IPAA (HealthyPouch) compared with chronic pouchitis (SickPouch), ulcerative colitis (UC), and a healthy intact colon microbiome (NormalGut). Furthermore, we investigated how repeated antibiotic use influences antimicrobial resistance on a bacterial genome level. Fecal samples from 190 participants were collected; HealthyPouch (n = 38), SickPouch (n = 37), UC (n = 23), and NormalGut (n = 92) and sequenced with Illumina and taxonomically profiled. Samples from HealthyPouch, SickPouch, and NormalGut were also long-read sequenced using Oxford Nanopore Technologies for reconstruction of 12 282 metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs). DNA methylation motifs were used for plasmid-host association. The HealthyPouch microbiome is distinct from both the UC, NormalGut, and SickPouch microbiome. Escherichia coli MAGs in the SickPouch (n = 21) microbiome had significantly higher co-occurring ciprofloxacin resistance mutations in the gyrA and parC genes, compared to both HealthyPouch (n = 26; BH adjusted P < .05) and NormalGut (n = 40; BH adjusted P < .05). Based on DNA methylation pattern, three plasmids were associated with E. coli carrying extended-spectrum beta lactamase genes. HealthyPouch microbiota differs from NormalGut microbiota, and could therefore be more appropriate for FMT treatment of chronic pouchitis. The association between E. coli and resistance gene-carrying plasmids underscores the importance of integrating plasmid analysis into metagenome-based approaches for personalized antibiotic treatment and resistance monitoring.

title: Quorum Sensing and Biofilm Regulation in ESKAPE Pathogens: Mechanisms, Therapeutic Targets, and Translational Challenges
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is an emerging global health threat responsible for antibiotics being ineffective, leading to persistent infections, increased mortality, and healthcare costs. ESKAPE (Enterococcus faecium, Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Acinetobacter baumannii, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Enterobacter species) pathogens have a higher priority worldwide for the development of therapeutic approaches other than traditional antibiotics. Quorum sensing (QS) links population-dependent gene expression with a mechanistic understanding of bacterial communication, virulence regulation, and biofilm-associated persistence. Major QS systems across ESKAPE pathogens are Agr and accessory gene regulator networks in Gram-positive bacteria; LuxS/AI-2 signaling; the LuxI/LuxR-family systems in Gram-negative bacteria; the Las, Rhl, and Pseudomonas quinolone signal (PQS) networks in P. aeruginosa; and the AbaI/AbaR system in A. baumannii. This review focuses on QS regulatory mechanisms in ESKAPE pathogens and discusses the novel approaches to target QS-associated virulence and biofilm formation. A review of the literature on QS signaling pathways, biofilm regulation, and anti-QS therapies was performed with special focus on combating strategies like plant-derived phytochemicals, synthetic QS inhibitors, enzymatic quorum quenching, probiotics, and combinations of QS-targeted agents with conventional antibiotics. QS systems are involved in virulence regulation, adhesion, biofilm maturation, and bacterial persistence. Plant-based compounds such as flavonoids, alkaloids, terpenoids, and polyphenols have been shown to have potential to interfere with QS-related processes. Synthetic inhibitors, quorum-quenching enzymes, probiotics, and antibiotic combination strategies are also promising approaches. By integrating QS regulation with virulence, biofilm biology, and antimicrobial response across ESKAPE pathogens, this review provides a comparative framework to guide future target prioritization, diagnostic development, and evaluation of adjunctive anti-virulence strategies. Mechanistic validation, standardized cross-pathogen comparisons, and long-term resistance-evolution studies are needed to establish the therapeutic readiness and clinical value of these approaches.

title: In vitro antibacterial and antibiofilm activity of phycocyanin against Klebsiella pneumoniae: effects on growth kinetics and antibiotic susceptibility
abstract: The increasing clinical burden of antimicrobial-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae, together with its capacity for biofilm formation and persistence, has intensified the search for alternative and adjunctive antimicrobial strategies. Phycocyanin is a cyanobacteria-derived phycobiliprotein with emerging biological and antimicrobial properties; however, its activity against K. pneumoniae, particularly across planktonic, biofilm, and antibiotic-response phenotypes, remains insufficiently characterized. Klebsiella pneumoniae ATCC 700,603 was used as the experimental strain, and phycocyanin obtained from Sigma was evaluated for antibacterial and antibiofilm activity. Minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) and minimum bactericidal concentration (MBC) were determined by broth microdilution and subsequent subculture, respectively. Bacterial growth kinetics were monitored for 72 h under sub-inhibitory phycocyanin exposure, while direct antibacterial activity was evaluated using an agar well diffusion assay. Biofilm formation was assessed using the crystal violet microtiter-plate method. Changes in antibiotic inhibition-zone diameters following sub-inhibitory phycocyanin exposure were evaluated using ampicillin, ceftriaxone, and imipenem. All experiments were performed in triplicate. Phycocyanin exhibited measurable antibacterial activity against K. pneumoniae, with MIC and MBC values of 10 and 20 mg/mL, respectively. Growth-kinetic analysis showed comparable bacterial growth during the initial hours, followed by sustained attenuation of growth in phycocyanin-exposed cultures from approximately 6 h onward. In the agar well diffusion assay, inhibition-zone diameters increased in a concentration-dependent manner, from approximately 7 mm at the lowest tested amount to 12 mm at the highest. Phycocyanin also inhibited biofilm formation in a concentration-dependent manner, with maximum inhibition reaching 41.3% at the highest tested concentration. Following sub-inhibitory phycocyanin exposure, increased inhibition-zone diameters were observed for ampicillin, ceftriaxone, and imipenem, with the greatest changes generally occurring after 24 h of exposure. Phycocyanin demonstrated antibacterial and concentration-dependent antibiofilm activity against K. pneumoniae ATCC 700,603 and altered the bacterial antibiotic-response phenotype following sub-inhibitory exposure. The observed effects on bacterial growth, biofilm formation, and antibiotic inhibition-zone diameters suggest that phycocyanin may have potential as an adjunctive antimicrobial or antibiofilm agent. However, these findings do not establish pharmacodynamic synergy or reversal of antimicrobial resistance. Further studies using quantitative combination assays, resistant clinical isolates, mechanistic approaches, and in vivo models are required to determine the translational relevance of these effects.

title: Transmission risk and mechanism of antibiotic resistance genes driven by glacier melt: Insight from Asian water tower to global significance
abstract: Accelerated glacier melt due to climate change is increasingly releasing sequestered antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs). However, ARG transmission risk and driven mechanisms that are associated with glacier retreat remain poorly understood. We employed genome-resolved metagenomics along a 246.5 km sampling transect spanning two distinct hydrological seasons and multiple habitats to track the dissemination of ARGs along the hydrological continuum of the Kuoqionggangri Glacier on Tibetan Plateau. Our results demonstrate that hydrological connectivity facilitates the physical transport of antibiotic resistant bacteria. Specific microbial lineages, particularly pathogenic Ralstonia pickettii were traced continuously from glacial sources to downstream rivers, disseminating both ARGs and virulence factors. Beyond host-mediated transport, glacier-derived ARGs can spread into downstream indigenous microbial communities via horizontal gene transfer. Genomic evidence confirmed that sulfonamide and β-lactam determinants transfer across taxonomic boundaries, disseminating from upstream environmental taxa (e.g., Novosphingobium) into downstream opportunistic pathogens. Finally, integrating 156 global glacier metagenomes revealed that the Tibetan Plateau yields an exceptionally high absolute ARG concentration (8.85 ± 0.07 log10 copies/L). Surpassing > 99% of the surveyed regions globally, the sheer magnitude of this genetic discharge identifies glacial melt as a critical emission hotspot, overwhelming downstream aquatic systems with severe ecological resistance risks.

title: The origin of Group B Streptococcus in Australian dogs, cats and cows
abstract: Streptococcus agalactiae, known in human medicine as Group B Streptococcus (GBS), affects numerous animal species, including dairy cattle and companion animals such as dogs and cats. In cattle, where GBS is a common cause of mastitis, host-specialist and host-generalist clades have been detected, whereas data on the origin of companion animal GBS is limited and somewhat contradictory. Here, we analyse a collection of 39 animal GBS isolates from Australia. Based on core genome analysis, the population composition matches the globally observed pattern of occurrence of host-specialist and host-generalist GBS in cattle, represented here by clonal complex 61/67 and sequence type (ST) 23, respectively, and host-generalist GBS in companion animals belonging to multiple sequence types and serotypes. Accessory genome analysis identifies non-exclusive but statistically significant and positive associations between the lactose operon and bovine isolates, and between the scpB gene or antimicrobial resistance genes and companion animal isolates. Proviral regions were detected in all isolates, whereby some phages or phage-inducible chromosomal islands (PICI) were associated with specific sequence types, e.g., phage E2 with ST67 from cattle and phage F2 with ST19 from companion animals. In agreement with results from Europe, our data suggest that GBS infections in dogs and cats are potentially derived from humans and may represent cases of reverse zoonosis.

title: Anthraquinone-enriched fraction of Rheum australe D. Don by Bioassay-guided fractionation and synergistic interaction with tetracycline against Bacterial pathogens
abstract: Rheum australe is an important medicinal herb known as Himalayan rhubarb. Traditionally used in Ayurveda and Tibetan medicine to treat diabetes, diarrhoea, hypertension, obesity, wounds, backache & gastrointestinal diseases. The current study is focused on studying the antibacterial and synergistic potential of the anthraquinone-enriched fraction of R. australe in combination with conventional antibiotics. The extract of R. australe was prepared using 70% ethanol with a Soxhlet apparatus, and Bioassay guided fractionation was done. Broth microdilution methods determined antibacterial and Synergistic activity of crude extracts and subfractions. Phytoconstituents were identified by LC-MS, and molecular docking was done to study the interaction with penicillin-binding protein 3, and docking-predicted potential interacting Phytoconstituents were quantified by HPLC. The extraction yield of the hydroalcoholic extract was recorded as 40.66 ± 3.05%. The chloroform subfraction showed the strongest antibacterial activity among all the subfractions against MRSA (64 μg/ mL), S. aureus (16 μg/mL) &P. aeruginosa (8 μg/mL) mL, and also the strongest synergistic activity with tetracycline against methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) (FICI 0.19-0.5), Staphylococcus aureus (FICI 0.0312-0.125), and Pseudomonas aeruginosa (FICI 0.125-0.375). Six phytoconstituents (piceatannol, chrysophanol, rhein, aloe-emodin, physcion & emodin) were identified by LC-MS. Molecular docking and MD simulation data revealed that among all the phytoconstituents, aloe-emodin, chrysophanol, emodin, & rhein indicated favourable interactions. HPLC analysis showed that these four phytoconstituents were enriched in the chloroform subfraction. The current study suggests that the chloroform subfraction enriched in anthraquinones exhibits strong antibacterial activity and synergistic activity in combination with tetracycline, and the synergistic mechanism of the combination remains to be established.

title: Combating drug-resistant Aeromonas veronii: Multiomics revealed the antibacterial mechanism of resveratrol
abstract: , widely distributed in aquatic ecosystems, is a prevalent fish pathogen and can cause human infections via contaminated aquatic products, polluted water contact, or tainted food consumption. Escalating antibiotic resistance instrains highlights an urgent need for alternative natural antimicrobial agents. This study investigated resveratrol's antibacterial mechanisms againstand evaluated its protective efficacy in hybrid sturgeon. Resveratrol exhibited strong activity [minimum inhibitory concentration: 128 microgram per milliliter (μg/ml), minimum bactericidal concentration: 256 μg/ml], disrupting cell wall/membrane integrity, inducing reactive oxygen species accumulation, inhibiting adenosine 5'-triphosphate synthesis, and down-regulating key metabolic pathways via transcriptomic and metabolomic analyses. In the sturgeon infection model, resveratrol-nanoemulsion notably improved survival, reduced tissue bacterial loads, mitigated oxidative stress and inflammation, and restored intestinal barrier function. These findings confirm resveratrol as a promising antibiotic alternative against, with nanoemulsion formulation enhancing its therapeutic efficacy.

title: Occurrence and Antimicrobial Resistance Profiles of ESBL-Producing Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae from Poultry Stool and Raw Meat in Rural and Urban Burkina Faso
abstract: Livestock contributes substantially to global food systems and livelihoods, particularly in low-income countries such as Burkina Faso. However, intensified poultry production has been associated with increased antibiotic use and the emergence of antimicrobial resistance (AMR). This study assessed the occurrence and antimicrobial resistance profiles of extended-spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL)-producingandisolated from poultry stool and raw meat samples collected in rural and urban areas of Burkina Faso. This cross-sectional study was conducted between February 2022 and December 2024 in Ouagadougou and Nouna. A total of 374 samples were collected, and the isolates were identified using biochemical testing and the VITEK 2 Compact system. ESBL production was confirmed using the combined-disk method according to EUCAST, 2022 guidelines. ESBL-producingandwere detected in 70 (18.7%; 95% CI: 15.0-23.1) and 25 (6.7%; 95% CI: 4.5-9.8) samples, respectively. Among poultry stool samples, ESBL-producingwere detected at similar frequencies in Ouagadougou and Nouna (Holm-adjusted= 0.250), whereas ESBL-producingwere detected significantly more frequently in Ouagadougou (Holm-adjusted= 0.004).showed high resistance to ampicillin (100%), tetracycline (90.0%), cefuroxime (84.3%), and ceftriaxone (81.4%). Allisolates were resistant to ampicillin, tetracycline, cefuroxime, ceftriaxone, and cotrimoxazole (100% each). Multidrug resistance was observed in 98.6% ofand 100% ofisolates. The detection of these organisms in the poultry production system and raw meat highlights the potential risk of foodborne transmission to humans. These findings underscore the need for improved antimicrobial stewardship, enhanced hygiene during slaughter and processing, and strengthened One Health surveillance strategies.

title: Investigating the multifaceted mechanism of hinokitiol: membrane perturbation and attenuation of quorum sensing-regulated virulence in Pseudomonas aeruginosa
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) has become a major global public health threat due to excessive use of antibiotics, requiring urgent attention to combat multidrug-resistant bacterial strains. In this context, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a clinically important opportunistic microbe, is widely known for causing persistent nosocomial infections due to its ability to form biofilms and secrete multiple quorum sensing (QS)-associated virulence factors. QS is a density-dependent communication system in bacteria that controls biofilm formation and pathogenic potential. Moreover, biofilm provides physical protection to the embedded bacteria from unfavorable conditions like chemicals, antimicrobial agents, pH, temperature, and UV light. In this study, we evaluated hinokitiol (HT) for its antimicrobial, anti-QS, and anti-biofilm activity against Pseudomonas aeruginosa. We also explored the underlying mechanism of action responsible for its growth and QS inhibition. Hinokitiol disrupted the membrane integrity and respiratory chain activity of bacteria at 50 and 100 µg/mL concentrations. In addition, it hinders biofilm formation at sub-inhibitory doses, which was confirmed by crystal violet assay, scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and fluorescence microscopy. Furthermore, qRT-PCR analysis showed that all four QS-related genes were downregulated in the presence of hinokitiol. Cytotoxicity analysis revealed that it shows dose-dependent toxicity towards mammalian cell lines, while lower concentrations (less than 25 µg/mL) exhibited no significant toxicity towards L6 cells even after prolonged exposure. These findings indicate that hinokitiol is a promising candidate to combat P. aeruginosa-associated infections.

title: Genomic Profiling of the Virulence Potential and Antimicrobial Resistance of Shiga Toxin-Producing Escherichia coli from Surface Water and Animal Sources
abstract: The aim of this work was to characterize the pathogenic potential of Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli (STEC) circulating in environmental and animal reservoirs. To achieve this, 225 genomes were analyzed: four genomes were obtained from bovine mastitis isolates, and 221 were obtained from the NCBI Pathogen Detection database originating from surface water and animal fecal samples. All genomes were analyzed to identify virulence-associated factors and antimicrobial resistance profiles in strains collected from surface water and animal samples. Virulence analysis revealed that stx1 and stx2 were detected in 32% and 44% of isolates, respectively. Environmental genomes frequently carried adhesion and LEE-associated genes, while mastitis isolates lacked these markers but exhibited enriched iron uptake systems and hemolysins, indicating niche-specific virulence repertoires. Resistance analysis identified 105 genes that contribute to antimicrobial resistance against multiple antibiotic families, including beta-lactams, quinolones, tetracyclines, aminoglycosides, and polymyxins. Phylogenetic analysis classified the strains mainly into phylogroups B1 (63.56%) and E (28%), and serotyping identified 41 serotypes, with O157:H7 being the most common (25.33%). MLST revealed 46 STs, with ST11 being the predominant one in animal fecal isolates. Overall, the data indicate a genetically diverse STEC population, with shared lineages among water, feces, and mastitis, as well as combined virulence and multidrug resistance profiles. This supports the need to incorporate genomic surveillance in environmental and livestock reservoirs to anticipate and mitigate the risks of transmission to the human population.

title: Molecular characteristics of Group B Streptococcus isolates from Daqing, Heilongjiang Province, China
abstract: Streptococcus agalactiae (Group B Streptococcus, GBS) is an important opportunistic pathogen associated with invasive infections in neonates, pregnant women, and immunocompromised adults, while increasing antimicrobial resistance poses challenges for clinical management. This study investigated the distribution, antimicrobial susceptibility, and molecular characteristics of GBS isolates collected from a tertiary hospital in Daqing, northeastern China. A total of 1,040 non-duplicate GBS isolates collected from outpatients and inpatients between 2020 and 2025 were analysed for specimen distribution and antimicrobial susceptibility. Molecular characterization was performed on 118 archived isolates using multiplex PCR for capsular serotypes, antimicrobial resistance genes, and virulence genes, together with the D-test for macrolide resistance phenotypes. The GBS carriage rate among women in late pregnancy was 6.0% (397/6,669). All isolates were susceptible to penicillin, ampicillin, vancomycin, linezolid, and tigecycline, while the resistance rates to erythromycin, clindamycin and levofloxacin were 93.2, 78, and 66.1%, respectively. Among the 118 characterised isolates, serotype Ib predominated (74.6%), followed by serotypes III (15.3%) and Ia (10.2%). The ermB (83.9%) and ermC (53.4%) genes were the predominant macrolide resistance determinants, and the constitutive MLSB (cMLSB) phenotype was the most common macrolide resistance phenotype (73.7%). These findings provide regional data on the antimicrobial susceptibility and molecular characteristics of GBS in northeastern China.

title: Recombinant outer-membrane vesicles (OMVs) from Salmonella Enteritidis as multivalent candidate vaccines for enteric fevers and invasive non-typhoidal Salmonella infections
abstract: Invasive non-typhoidal(iNTS) infections, typhoid, and paratyphoid fever are major global health burdens, particularly considering increasing antimicrobial resistance. These diseases often colocalize geographically, making broadly protective multivalent vaccines highly desirable. Multicomponent vaccine candidates are currently being developed to achieve protection against multiple systemicdiseases.The aim of this study was to create a vaccine candidate against iNTS and typhoid fever consisting of bacterial outer-membrane vesicles (OMVs) expressing simultaneously multiple key immunogenic antigens on their membrane surface.The abequose synthase () gene was inserted intoEnteritidis to achieve expression of the O:4 surface polysaccharide antigen, alongside the naturally expressed O:9 antigen. The Vi polysaccharide was expressed using a plasmid containing theoperon. Reactogenicity of lipopolysaccharide molecules was reduced by deleting theandgenes to alter Lipid A acylation. Thegene was deleted to increase the yield of OMVs by the mutant bacteria. Immunization of mice with the O:4, O:9, and Vi-expressing OMVs resulted in antibody responses against all three target antigens and reduced bacterial burdens in the livers and spleens of the animals after challenging with virulentTyphimurium andEnteritidis.

title: Bridging generalizability and reproducibility in machine learning-based antimicrobial resistance prediction
abstract: The rapid growth of whole-genome sequencing and machine learning (ML) has led to a multitude of methods for predicting antimicrobial resistance (AMR) from bacterial genomic data. Despite increasingly high reported predictive performance, substantial differences in data sets, phenotype definitions, genomic preprocessing, evaluation strategies, and validation procedures make it difficult to determine whether models will perform reliably beyond the data on which they were developed. In machine learning, this problem is generally framed in terms of generalizability: the ability of a model to maintain performance when applied to previously unseen data. In microbiology, many of the same considerations ultimately manifest as a problem of reproducibility. In this review, we provide a brief overview of the fundamental concepts underlying machine learning-based AMR prediction and then examine the factors that affect model generalizability and reproducibility.

title: Annual hospital antibiograms in low- and middle-income countries: far from obsolete, not yet achieved
Innovative β-lactams and β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor combinations against carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales
abstract: SUMMARYThe global dissemination of carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales (CPE) represents one of the most pressing threats to modern antimicrobial therapy. The rapid worldwide expansion of these organisms has been driven by the emergence and successful dissemination of diverse carbapenemases belonging to Ambler classes A, B, and D, including KPC, OXA-48-like, and metallo-β-lactamases, such as NDM, VIM, and IMP. These enzymes severely compromise the activity of carbapenems, historically considered the cornerstone for treatment of severe infections caused by multidrug-resistant Gram-negative bacteria. In response to this growing challenge, substantial efforts in antibiotic discovery have led to the development of several novel β-lactams and β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor combinations specifically designed to restore activity against carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales (CRE). This review provides a comprehensive microbiological overview of recently approved and investigational agents targeting CPE. We examine the structural and mechanistic features of key therapeutic options, including cefiderocol and multiple β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor combinations incorporating classical penicillin-based sulfone derivatives, diazabicyclooctanes, and cyclic boronates. Particular attention is given to the biochemical properties and inhibitory spectra of β-lactamase inhibitors, as well as the antimicrobial activity of novel β-lactams and β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor combinations against both isogenic strains and large collections of clinical Enterobacterales isolates. In addition, we discuss the emerging resistance mechanisms that may compromise the clinical effectiveness of these agents. Understanding the mechanistic basis of both activity and resistance is essential to guide their optimal therapeutic positioning and to inform the next generation of antimicrobial development aimed at combating the ongoing threat of CRE.

title: Draft genome sequences of four Escherichia coli strains from lake water in Dhaka, Bangladesh
abstract: The draft genomes of four environmentalstrains reveal potentially pathogenic strains, along with mobile genetic elements, antibiotic resistance genes, and numerous prophage regions, suggesting genetically diversepopulations in Bangladesh's freshwater environments.

title: Off-panel resistance determinants in a high-resistance setting: comparative evaluation of syndromic multiplex PCR, metagenomic sequencing, and phenotypic AST in bloodstream infections
abstract: Rapid syndromic molecular panels substantially reduce turnaround time for bloodstream infection diagnosis by identifying common pathogens and selected antimicrobial resistance determinants directly from positive blood cultures. However, their fixed target repertoires may limit diagnostic coverage in settings with diverse endemic resistance mechanisms and clinically relevant off-panel organisms. This retrospective comparative diagnostic study evaluated direct-from-positive-blood-culture metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS), the BioFire Blood Culture Identification 2 (BCID2) panel, and routine microbiological methods across 165 positive blood-culture episodes from 145 patients at a tertiary-care center with a high burden of antimicrobial resistance. Complete recovery of the routine-culture organism set was achieved in 155/165 episodes (93.9%) by mNGS and 142/165 (86.1%) by BCID2. Among 23 episodes with incomplete routine-set recovery by BCID2, mNGS restored complete coverage in 18 (78.3%). For meropenem resistance, sensitivity was numerically higher with mNGS than with BCID2 (90.0% versus 75.0%), whereas ceftriaxone-resistance sensitivity among Enterobacterales was numerically higher with BCID2 (97.5% versus 85.0%); neither paired difference was statistically significant. BCID2 meropenem very major errors were concentrated among non-fermenting gram-negative organisms, particularly, and were frequently associated with off-paneldetected by mNGS. Overall, targeted syndromic testing and mNGS demonstrated complementary diagnostic performance, with mNGS extending organism and resistance-mechanism coverage beyond predefined molecular targets, while phenotypic antimicrobial susceptibility testing remained necessary for definitive susceptibility assessment.IMPORTANCERapid molecular blood-culture panels provide clinically actionable results, but are inherently restricted to predefined pathogen and resistance targets. This limitation is particularly relevant in regions where local antimicrobial resistance epidemiology includes mechanisms not represented within commercial panel repertoires. In this study, metagenomic sequencing improved recovery of routine-culture organisms and identified off-panel carbapenem resistance determinants underlying several false-susceptible panel results, particularly OXA-23 in. However, broader genomic detection did not consistently improve phenotypic resistance prediction across antimicrobial classes. These findings illustrate that diagnostic breadth and phenotypic predictive accuracy are distinct attributes and support the use of metagenomic sequencing as a complementary approach to rapid targeted testing and conventional antimicrobial susceptibility testing.

title: Draft genome sequences of Vibrio cholerae C6706 isolates evolved under erythromycin and tetracycline selection
abstract: We report draft genome sequences of sixC6706 isolates evolvedto an eightfold increase in tetracycline or erythromycin MIC, with three independent lineages per antibiotic. Assemblies comprised 110 to 130 contigs totaling 4.01 to 4.02 Mb, each estimated 100% complete by CheckM2.

title: Mycoplasma genitalium extracellular vesicles and the P140 adhesin carboxyl region as high-fidelity antigens for improved serodiagnosis
abstract: () is an important etiological agent of sexually transmitted infections that has emerged as a global health threat. Despite its clinical importance, accurate serodiagnosis remains challenging due to high cross-reactivity caused by non-specific proteins. To address this limitation, we optimizedgrowth in a serum-free minimal medium to characterize the biogenesis and diagnostic applications of-secreted extracellular vesicles (EVs). We demonstrate thatgenerates EVs that retain immunodominant proteins, specifically the key adhesins P140 and P110. From an initial cohort of 1,608 women (12.5%positive), we selected a longitudinal sub-study population, including 24 women who were PCR-positive at enrollment and a control group of 14 individuals who remained-negative across three visits, each spaced approximately 6 months apart. Comparative ELISA and immunoblotting using sera from-infected and uninfected individuals revealed that the EV-associated antigens provide superior diagnostic discrimination over conventional total-cell lysates and lipid-associated membrane protein extracts. Notably, EV-associated antigens lack common non-specific proteins, such as immunoglobulin-binding protein, MG281. Functional characterization using full-length and truncated P140 variants in cell-based ELISAs with human cervical epithelial cells identified the C-terminal region (P140-C) as the primary host-cell-interacting domain. In addition, this specific region induces an epitope-restricted antibody response in infected individuals. Within the longitudinal clinical cohort, high anti-P140-C antibody titers correlated with a trend towardclearance, suggesting potential prognostic utility despite lacking statistical significance. Collectively, these results establishEVs as a high-fidelity antigenic source and identify P140-C as a promising candidate for the development of next-generation serological assays. Serodiagnosis of(Mg) faces significant challenges, especially in the context of emerging antimicrobial resistance and asymptomatic infections. This study introduces-derived extracellular vesicles (EVs) as a source of refined antigens for serodiagnosis. By isolating the P140 C-terminal region, we identified a highly specific marker that overcomes antigenic variation, reduces cross-reactivity, and offers a candidate antigen that may warrant evaluation as a marker of infection clearance. By leveraging bacterial EVs as a source of purified diagnostic antigen, our findings offer a framework with broader implications for other antigenically complex pathogens.

title: Draft genome sequence of Escherichia coli SAU_MI_1GVS2 isolated from a goat vaginal swab in Dhaka, Bangladesh
abstract: We describe the draft genome sequence ofSAU_MI_1GVS2, isolated from a goat vaginal swab in Dhaka, Bangladesh. Sequencing with the Illumina NextSeq platform generated a 4.98 Mb genome with 4,619 coding sequences, including genes associated with putative antibiotic resistance and virulence.

title: Pseudomonas sediminis CRE-TB-54 carries tmexCD3-toprJ3 in a novel chromosomal region
abstract: The emergence of tmexCD-toprJ, coding for a transmissible multidrug resistance efflux pump of the resistance-nodulation-division (RND) family has compromised the usefulness of tigecycline in the treatment of infections caused by multidrug resistant Gram-negative bacteria. Here, we describe the presence of tmexCD3-toprJ3 in a novel chromosomal context in Pseudomonas sediminis CRE-TB-54 isolated from a toilet in a university dormitory in southwestern Nigeria. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing and whole genome sequencing showed that CRE-TB-54 displayed intermediate level resistance to tigecycline and haboured multiple antibiotic resistance genes, including tmexCD3-toprJ3 flanked upstream and downstream by genetic structures not previously reported in association with tmexCD-toprJ. These include insertion sequences IS4 and IS30, and the metal resistance gene czcD upstream, the prophage integrase IntA, the competence associated DNA binding protein gene comEA, and the double stranded DNA repair and homologous recombination gene cluster recBCD downstream. These results provide new insight into the genetic structures surrounding the tmexCD-toprJ cluster and raises concern about toilets as a potential environmental reservoir of bacteria carrying this clinically important gene in a resource-limited setting where tigecycline is not currently used in human or animals.

title: Genomic analysis of extended-spectrum β-lactamase-producing Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae isolated from a dog with a severe episode of self-trauma and urinary tract infection
abstract: Extended-spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL)-producing Enterobacterales are emerging pathogens of major importance in veterinary medicine. This study describes the clinical, microbiological, and genomic characteristics of ESBL-producing Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae isolated from a dog with paraparesis and concurrent pyelonephritis, chronic cystitis, and a self-traumatized limb lesion. A 12-year-old mixed-breed female dog underwent repeated antimicrobial therapy during hospitalization. Urine obtained by cystocentesis and wound samples were cultured, and ESBL-producing strains were characterized by antimicrobial susceptibility testing and whole-genome sequence-based analysis. CTX-M-55-producing E. coli sequence type (ST) 457, phylogroup F, O11:H25, and fimH145, was recovered from urine and wound samples, while the wound sample also yielded a CTX-M-15- and SHV-2-producing K. pneumoniae ST39, KL149:OL2α.2. The two closely related E. coli strains differed by 96 single nucleotide polymorphisms, despite sharing the same ST, resistome, plasmid replicons, and virulence profile. ESBL-positive strains carried multiple virulence genes, with the E. coli strains classified as extraintestinal pathogenic E. coli strains. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first report of ESBL-producing K. pneumoniae ST39 in an animal in Brazil. The co-occurrence of ESBL-producing E. coli ST457 and K. pneumoniae ST39 in the same dog highlights the potential for companion animals to harbor clinically relevant multidrug-resistant lineages and reinforces the need for continuous antimicrobial resistance monitoring and antimicrobial stewardship in this sector.

title: Developing a digital knowledge-to-practice framework for urinary device management and CAUTI surveillance
abstract: Inappropriate urinary device use and catheter-associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI) contribute to preventable patient harm, antimicrobial resistance, incontinence-associated dermatitis (IAD) and prolonged hospitalisation. To describe the development, implementation and evaluation of a digitally enabled urinary device knowledge-to-practice framework designed to strengthen clinical governance, improve CAUTI surveillance and support harm prevention. A practice-based implementation programme was led by the Continence Lead Nurse at University Hospitals of Leicester NHS Trust. Following an evidence review, the Continence Lead Nurse independently undertook a prospective clinical audit of CAUTI symptoms and microbiology findings. The audit informed the decision to embed CAUTI symptom prompts within electronic catheter care plans and develop CAUTIon+, a digital surveillance dashboard. Evidence-based urinary device pathways and digital care plans were integrated into trust-wide clinical policy. A female external catheter (FEC) pathway was evaluated through a 6-week feasibility study and a separate 6-month value-based procurement evaluation. Implementation established daily prospective CAUTI surveillance through CAUTIon+, supporting earlier identification of suspected infection and structured clinical review. In the initial FEC evaluation, all nine patients reported positive experiences, while 19 of 21 staff respondents highly recommended the device. The subsequent procurement evaluation recorded a 93% reduction in IAD cases (43 to 3), with an estimated 132 bed days avoided and £67 896.30 in reported net savings. Integrating digital urinary device care plans, trust-wide clinical policy and CAUTIon+ surveillance translated evidence into routine practice and strengthened urinary device stewardship. The framework supports earlier clinical intervention and antimicrobial stewardship, with the potential to contribute to prevention of urinary-source sepsis. It aligns with the NHS 10-year health plan's shift towards digital, preventive health care and offers a model for wider NHS evaluation.

title: Draft genome sequence of Escherichia coli ECMC01 isolated from clinical bovine mastitis in Malaysia
abstract: The draft genome sequence ofECMC01 isolated from bovine mastitis in Malaysia is reported. The 5.13-Mb genome encodes 4,967 predicted protein-coding genes, 92 RNA genes, and multiple determinants associated with antimicrobial resistance and virulence.

title: Antimicrobial-resistant Urinary Tract Infections in Febrile Infants: Prevalence, Associated Factors and Clinical Outcomes
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance among pediatric urinary tract infections (UTIs) has become an increasing concern. However, data regarding resistant infections in febrile infants remain limited. We performed a retrospective single-center study including febrile infants younger than 24 months diagnosed with UTI in a pediatric emergency department in Spain between March 2022 and August 2025. Clinical, microbiologic and outcome-related variables were compared according to antimicrobial susceptibility. Bivariate and multivariate logistic regression analyses were performed to identify predictors of resistant infection. Among 336 UTI episodes, resistant microorganisms were identified in 36 (10.7%). Escherichia coli was the predominant pathogen (303/336, 90.2%), accounting for 270/300 susceptible infections and 33/36 resistant infections. Multidrug-resistant and extended-spectrum β-lactamase-producing organisms accounted for most resistant isolates (28/36, 77.8%; and 14/36, 38.9%, respectively), and 8/36 (22.2%) fulfilled criteria for both phenotypes. No carbapenem-resistant organisms were identified. Baseline characteristics did not differ significantly between groups. No independent predictors of resistant infection were identified in the multivariate analysis. Resistant infections were associated with a higher proportion of adverse outcomes (33.3% vs. 15.3%; P = 0.01), mainly recurrences, although this finding was attenuated in the sensitivity analysis restricted to first episodes (27.3% vs. 14.9%; P = 0.08). Approximately 1 in 10 UTIs in febrile infants were caused by resistant microorganisms. No independent predictors were identified. Resistant infections were associated with a higher proportion of adverse outcomes, mainly recurrences, although this finding should be interpreted cautiously. Further prospective studies incorporating molecular typing techniques are needed to better characterize antimicrobial resistance dynamics in recurrent pediatric UTIs.

title: Comparative genomic and resistome analysis of Citrobacter koseri: first genome report from Egypt
abstract: Citrobacter koseri is increasingly implicated in healthcare- and community-associated infections, with multidrug-resistant (MDR) strains posing a growing clinical concern. However, its population structure and resistome dynamics remain incompletely understood. Here, we report the first draft genome sequence of an MDR C. koseri isolate (DFU32) from Egypt, recovered from a patient with a diabetic foot ulcer (DFU). We also present a comparative genomic and resistome analysis of 518 publicly available C. koseri genomes available at the time of the study. The isolate exhibited resistance to multiple antimicrobial classes, including β-lactams, aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, and sulfonamides, as well as tigecycline and colistin. MLST assigned DFU32 to sequence type (ST) 1172. Genomic analysis identified 21 antimicrobial resistance (AMR) genes, including multiple β-lactamases (bla, bla, bla, bla, and bla) and aminoglycoside resistance determinants, including armA. Colistin resistance was associated with the presence of a PhoQ V381I substitution. Comparative analysis of 518 publicly available genomes revealed 140 unique AMR genes across the species, with 73.6% of genomes carrying acquired resistance determinants. The population comprised two major lineages, blaand bla, with the MAL lineage, particularly MAL-2, carrying significantly more AMR genes. Carbapenemase genes were identified in 29.1% of genomes and were distributed across nearly half of the detected STs, with blavariants predominating. Mobilized colistin resistance (mcr) genes were detected in 2.5% of genomes. Both carbapenemase and mcr genes were predominantly located on plasmid-associated contigs. Notably, chromosomal integration events were observed. These included mcr-9.1, which was associated with IS26 and IS903B, and bla, which was embedded within an IS26-bracketed transposon (IS26-recA-ISKpn27-bla-ISKpn6-IS26) in novel STs. These findings underscore the genomic plasticity of C. koseri and the potential for stable, plasmid-independent maintenance of colistin and carbapenem resistance. Among the identified STs, ST690 displayed a particularly high resistance gene load, including carbapenemase and mcr genes, suggesting that it may represent a high-risk lineage. This study provides the first genome-based characterization of an MDR C. koseri isolate from Egypt. The results highlight the potential genetic mobility and global spread of AMR determinants in this emerging pathogen. Notably, the studied isolate was recovered from DFU, underscoring the increasing clinical relevance of C. koseri in chronic wound infections.

title: In silico identification of drug compounds to arabinose-5-phosphate isomerase of Proteus mirabilis to combat its antibiotic resistance using an integrated bioinformatics: subtractive proteomics, molecular docking, MD simulation and DFT studies
abstract: Proteus mirabilis is a major opportunistic Gram-negative pathogen causing complicated urinary tract infections (UTIs), particularly in catheterized patients. Although several antibiotics, including streptomycin, erythromycin, and sparfloxacin, remain effective against some infections, the growing spread of multidrug-resistant P. mirabilis strains has created an urgent need to identify new therapeutic targets and treatment options. Using a subtractive proteomics approach, this study identified potential therapeutic targets in P. mirabilis. Among the 417 essential pathogen-specific proteins, 11 were identified as druggable, virulence-associated, and antibiotic resistance-related proteins, making them promising novel therapeutic targets against P. mirabilis. Among them, nine are enzymatic proteins involved in crucial biological pathways such as glycan and amino acid biosynthesis, energy metabolism, cellular signaling, and genetic information processing. The protein-protein interactions (PPIs) and hub gene analysis revealed arabinose-5-phosphate isomerase (API) as a primary target; structure-guided virtual screening identified five hits, ferric derisomaltose, hyaluronic acid, acarbose, rutin, and dihydrostreptomycin that exhibit binding affinities ranging from -13.540 to -10.616 kcal/mol with P. mirabilis arabinose-5-phosphate isomerase (PmAPI), suggesting their potential as anti-P. mirabilis agents towards infectious disease control. The density functional theory (DFT) studies and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations interaction analysis on PmAPI with potent hits clearly showed reactivity of the hits and stable binding with PmAPI during the 500-ns MD simulation.

title: Influenza vaccination in people with diabetes mellitus: Clinical rationale, current evidence, and implementation challenges
abstract: People with diabetes mellitus (DM) are at increased risk of hospitalisation, complications, and mortality from influenza due to immune dysfunction, metabolic imbalance, and a higher incidence of cardiovascular events. This narrative review, targeted at clinical practice in Spain, summarises recent evidence on diabetes and influenza vaccination and explores barriers to its implementation. Evidence shows that annual vaccination in people with DM reduces hospitalisations, cardiovascular events, and mortality, particularly in those aged ≥ 60 years or with comorbidities; higher-immunogenicity formulations (high-dose or adjuvanted) may provide an additional benefit in these populations. In addition, coadministration with other adult vaccines is feasible. Person-centred recommendations for endocrinology and general practice are proposed to improve suboptimal coverage. Influenza vaccination is cost-effective and may help reduce inappropriate antibiotic use and antimicrobial resistance in this population.

title: Global Genomic Analysis of Antimicrobial Resistance in Streptococcus pyogenes
abstract: Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A Streptococcus, GAS) is a major global pathogen. While macrolide resistance has been studied, large-scale analyses of overall antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in GAS across geographic datasets remain limited. This study aimed to comprehensively investigate AMR in GAS over more than a century. A total of 47,689 high-quality S. pyogenes genomes from 59 countries, collected between 1900 and 2025 (predominantly post-1990), underwent quality control. Multilocus sequence typing and in silico prediction of AMR determinants using AMRFinderPlus v4.2.5 were performed. Temporal trends were analyzed via quasibinomial regression. Phenotypic susceptibility data from 310 isolates were interpreted using CLSI 2023 breakpoints. GAS showed high genomic conservation (mean genome size, ∼1.81 Mb; ∼1,705 coding sequences). The non-macrolide resistome was dominated by tetracycline and aminoglycoside-associated genes, with tet(M) being the most prevalent (20.96%), followed by aph(3')-IIIa (8.50%), sat4 (8.30%), and ant(6)-Ia (7.69%). Overtime, the prevalence of sat4, aph(3')-IIIa, ant(6)-Ia, and tet(M) increased significantly, whereas that of tet(L), tet(O), and pbp2x_P601L declined (P < 0.05). Reduced susceptibility to selected β-lactams (cefuroxime, imipenem, meropenem) was sporadic (3-10%), primarily linked to pbp2x_P601L, whereas penicillin retained near-universal activity (99.7% susceptibility). Typical β-lactamase genes were rare and geographically restricted. Phenotypic resistance was detected for tetracycline (6%) and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (4%), with 13% showing intermediate susceptibility to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. S. pyogenes remains highly susceptible to penicillin and other β-lactams. Resistance is mainly associated with tetracycline and aminoglycoside genes, which show dynamic changes over time due to ongoing selection pressures.
